articles.title: As World Bank Retreats From Climate Targets, India’s Most Vulnerable Could Pay the Price
articles.full_text:
Most climate finance goes where it is easiest to lend. Embankments, water systems, shade, and shelters that save lives and livelihoods in villages struggle to find funding.
A man carries a calf through flood waters in Assam’s Dibrugarh district, India, July 2024.
More than 80 percent of India’s population lives in districts highly vulnerable to floods, droughts, and cyclones, according to the Climate Vulnerability Index developed by the Council on Energy, Environment and Water. In states such as Assam, Andhra Pradesh, Maharashtra, Karnataka, and Bihar, that vulnerability is already visible in damaged roads, disrupted farming, and recurring displacement. Local officials know what is needed — higher roads, stronger embankments, safer shelters, and simple early-warning systems. However, the problem is not knowledge, but funding.
Just as these districts need more protection from rising heat and encroaching water, the World Bank has ended its 45 percent climate finance target, a change that could weaken accountability for where money goes. This decision will widen the gap between where climate money is easiest to spend and where it is actually needed. For India’s poorest, most climate‑exposed districts, especially marginalized rural communities, dropping a binding target weakens accountability and makes it easier to bury real adaptation needs under vague “outcomes.”
When there is no hard number to meet, money is more likely to flow toward large, easy-to-package projects such as solar parks, grid upgrades, and metro lines. The risk is that large projects are counted as climate work while flood-prone districts wait for funds for embankments, shelters, or early-warning systems.
We write this as researchers and advocates who have worked inside government and policy settings and seen how funding commitments shrink as they move from paper to practice.
At COP28 in Dubai, the World Bank set a simple rule: 45 percent of its annual financing would support projects with climate co-benefits, meaning work that either cuts emissions or helps people cope with floods, heat, and drought. The 45 percent climate co-benefits target asked a simple question: how much of the Bank’s lending was meaningfully climate related?
In June, under pressure from the United States, the Bank said it would retire that 45 percent target. It now says it will stop counting how much of its lending is climate-related and instead focus on broader “outcomes to maximize development impact,” with climate supposedly woven into everything it does.
On paper, that may sound flexible. But without a clear benchmark, it becomes harder for outsiders, including India, to check what is actually being financed or whether the money is reaching the places that need it most.
India needs substantial climate finance each year: about $160 billion to $288 billion annually through 2030 just to keep up with climate change. Flood barriers, drought relief, and heat-resilient homes matter just as much as mitigation projects. But the finance reaching adaptation work on the ground remains far below what is needed, and states are stuck with strained budgets, borrowing limits, and no steady pipeline of support to count on.
Most climate finance still goes where it is easiest to lend: grid upgrades, solar parks, wind farms, transmission lines, and green hydrogen. These usually sit in or near big cities and industrial corridors. Meanwhile, the smaller projects that save lives in villages and districts — embankments, water systems, shade, cooling centers, and shelters — struggle to find funding. Wealthy nations have repeatedly promised to close this gap, but the shortfall remains. For most Indian states, cheap long-term loans and guarantees from major lenders remain the only realistic path to real climate protection. So, when the World Bank weakens firm climate commitments, these states are left wondering how they will cover even the basics.
The neglected districts are home to Dalit, Adivasi, and other marginalized communities, often landless laborers and informal workers. Their voices rarely shape how public money gets spent. It is also hard to track whether adaptation funds ever actually reach them. A hard number in climate lending gave activists, journalists, and local leaders something to point to. Take the number away, and these communities are being asked to trust a system that has often put them last in line.
The World Bank itself argues that projects with climate co-benefits are “smart development” and says it is shifting from measuring climate inputs to measuring outcomes across its broader portfolio. That sounds plausible, but in an unequal system the loss of a floor can quickly become the loss of a priority. For India’s marginalized districts, flexibility without a hard minimum may simply mean more delay for the projects that matter most.
If the World Bank wants to prove that retiring its climate target is not a retreat, India should ask for two concrete commitments in return. First, a public guarantee that a fixed share of climate lending reaches the most exposed districts and communities. Second, transparent, publicly auditable reporting on where every climate rupee goes, so climate finance can be tracked for equity.
From a meeting room in Washington, the new era may look like smart, flexible development. From a flooded panchayat (local government) office in Bihar, it looks like an embankment, shelter, or warning system pushed further out of reach.

articles.title: KMT, TPP Mull Referendums to Go With Taiwan’s Local Elections
articles.full_text:
Up to six proposals – ranging from nuclear power to absentee voting – will be put to voters in the November polls, but without the usual round of campaigning for signatures.
Taiwan’s local elections – often referred to as “nine-in-one elections,” due to voting taking place simultaneously for nine different kinds of positions – will soon be upon us, with voting scheduled for the end of November. Alongside the elections, however, a number of referendum issues will also be voted on nationally. 
The referendums are advanced by the Kuomintang (KMT) and the Taiwan People’s Party (TPP), the opposition parties currently in control of the legislature. However, unlike past referendums, the KMT and TPP will not campaign with the general public for signatures to get these motions on the ballot. Instead, the KMT and TPP intend to use their combined majority in the legislature to initiate the referendums as a chamber resolution. Consequently, six referendums will take place simultaneously with the local elections. 
One issue that is to be voted on is a familiar one – nuclear energy. Specifically, the KMT calls for the abolishment of policies to enact a nuclear-free homeland. Since the Fukushima nuclear disaster in Japan, Taiwan has been phasing out the use of nuclear power by not extending the lifespan of nuclear reactors. Taiwan’s last operating nuclear reactor thus shut down in May 2025.
Opposing the use of nuclear energy in Taiwan has been a traditional stance of the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP), the Lai administration has submitted plans for the restart of two reactors. The Lai administration’s shift on nuclear energy may be due to concerns about Taiwan’s energy supply, which is highly reliant on liquefied natural gas, being cut off in the event of an invasion or blockade. There are also concerns internationally about the energy supply that Taiwan needs in order to continue to fuel the AI boom with its semiconductor manufacturing. 
That U-turn may take the wind out of the sails of the KMT’s nuclear energy referendum, even if the Lai administration claims that its eventual goal to phase out nuclear remain unchanged, and nuclear energy will be used alongside renewables. 
Likewise, the KMT has called for a referendum on capital punishment. This is another issue that the KMT has often leveraged in past years, with polls consistently showing high public support for capital punishment in Taiwan.
A Constitutional Court ruling in September 2024 narrowed the scope of the application of capital punishment but did not abolish it. An execution was carried out in January 2025, the first in five years. The KMT has consistently framed the DPP as having enacted a de facto moratorium on capital punishment. But because capital punishment is still on the books in Taiwan, a previous attempt by the KMT to hold a referendum calling for its reinstatement was thrown out in 2025 by the Central Election Commission (CEC). 
Another punitive proposal from the KMT would be to hold a referendum on the implementation of caning as a punishment for serious crimes such as child abuse, sexual assault, and fraud. This is an unusual proposal, seeing as there was no previous demand from society that caning should be implemented as a legal punishment in order to deter crime. 
Critics of the referendum have warned that implementing caning – mostly used as a legal punishment in countries with Sharia law or former British colonies – would fall afoul of human rights conventions that Taiwan has ratified. Perhaps cautious of the perception that the caning referendum is out of left field, KMT chair Cheng Li-wun previously tried to take the caning referendum off the agenda. However, pushback from the party’s legislative caucus led to the KMT continuing to advocate for it. 
A fourth proposal would allow for medical euthanasia to take place in Taiwan. Medical euthanasia has been increasingly discussed in Taiwan in past years, but there is no clear social consensus on the issue. Support for or opposition to medical euthanasia is not an issue that divides cleanly along party lines, making the referendum an important gauge as to what social views on euthanasia are in Taiwan. 
The fifth proposal to be voted on pertains to traffic safety. Specifically, the proposal, as advanced by the TPP, calls for allocating fines from traffic violations to local governments, as earmarked for road safety improvements and transportation subsidies. The proposal may be framed along the lines of traffic safety, increasingly a concern at a time that Taiwan has been criticized as a “pedestrian hell.” But the proposal can perhaps be understood as in line with continued contestation between the pan-Blue and pan-Green camps about the budget, with the pan-Blue controlled legislature seeking to drastically cut funding to the DPP-controlled central government, and pan-Blue mayors criticizing that the central government cut subsidies to local governments in response to the budget reductions. Pan-Green critics have suggested that there is no need for a referendum on this issue when the KMT and TPP could simply pass laws to make such changes. 
The sixth proposal, on absentee voting, was also advanced by the TPP. The proposal would allow absentee voting for national elections – although it would not permit voting from overseas, which would be highly contentious. There have been long fears about the impact on Taiwanese elections if taishang, Taiwanese businessmen residing in China, were allowed to vote from overseas. It is often assumed that they would vote in line with what China wants or that this could open the door to Chinese election interference. 
Instead, under the TPP proposal, absentee balloting would only occur from within Taiwan, where many people do not reside in their voting districts. While voting district is tied to household registration, tax policy often makes landlords unwilling to allow tenants to update their household registration to match rented apartments or homes. 
This proposal has been criticized openly by CEC chair Michael You as potentially leading to chaos. With the KMT and DPP alike having built up party machines around campaigning with the current set-up – in which voters often do not live where they vote – both parties may be hesitant to rethink this. As a newer party, the TPP may benefit, however, from a shaking up of the present election system. 
The KMT is probably hoping to replicate its successes in the 2018 elections, when the party was seen as successfully capitalizing on a national referendum in order to have successes in local elections. At the same time, there was blowback in 2018 over the large number of referendum questions leading to confusion at the polls, and long lines for voting even after polls closed. In order to avoid this happening again, the KMT and TPP have proposed legislation to put multiple referendum questions on one ballot, so as to avoid confusion in paperwork. 
Holding national referendums without a significant period of public campaigning for signatures is relatively untested in Taiwan, even if legal changes passed in the last decade have made it easier to hold referendums than ever. As such, it is to be seen whether the KMT and TPP are able to replicate their past successes in preceding election cycles. For now, the debate over the referendums is a small preview of the elections later this year.

articles.title: Japan’s 2026 Defense White Paper Warns of China’s Expanding Military Reach in the Pacific
articles.full_text:
This year’s white paper places particular emphasis on Beijing’s growing ability to project military power beyond the First Island Chain.
The Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force’s second Izumo-class helicopter carrier Kaga, whose bow has been modified to a rectangular shape to enable operations of the stealth F-35B fighter.
On August 4, Japan’s Cabinet approved the 2026 edition of its annual defense white paper, warning that China is steadily expanding its military reach into the Pacific beyond the First Island Chain, the strategic arc linking Japan’s southwestern islands, Taiwan, and the Philippines. 
The report, Defense of Japan 2026, again described China as “an unprecedented and the greatest strategic challenge” to Japan’s peace and security, repeating language first adopted in Japan’s revised National Security Strategy in 2022. This year’s white paper placed particular emphasis on China’s expanding military activities in the Pacific, highlighting what Tokyo views as Beijing’s growing ability to project military power beyond the so-called First Island Chain and increasingly deeper into the Pacific.
The report argued that these challenges should be addressed by strengthening Japan’s “comprehensive national power,” together with closer cooperation with allies and like-minded partners. It also emphasized lessons from modern warfare and the need to reinforce Japan’s defense industrial base.
The white paper said that China’s People’s Liberation Army (PLA) has become increasingly active around Japan in the East China Sea, the Sea of Japan, and the western Pacific beyond the First Island Chain.
According to the report, these operations are intended not only to improve the PLA’s combat capabilities but also to create a “fait accompli” by establishing a regular military presence in the area.
“Repeated joint activities are obviously intended as demonstration activities against Japan and pose a grave concern for Japan’s security,” the report stated.
A newly added graphic section highlighted China’s expanding military activities in the Pacific, including aircraft carrier deployments, long-range naval operations, and other activities beyond the First Island Chain.
It cited the deployment of the aircraft carrier Liaoning east of Iwo Jima in June 2025 and subsequent carrier operations in the Pacific – including its first confirmed operations beyond the Second Island Chain, which stretches from Japan’s Izu and Ogasawara islands to Guam and Saipan – underscoring what Tokyo sees as China’s growing ability to sustain naval and air operations farther from its coastline.
The report also referred to an incident in which a Chinese military aircraft repeatedly targeted a Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force patrol aircraft with a laser for about 30 minutes over the Pacific east of Okinawa.
Taiwan also featured prominently. The white paper noted that China has repeatedly conducted large-scale military exercises around Taiwan since 2022. The report argued that the exercises are intended both to increase military pressure on Taiwan and improve the PLA’s operational capabilities.
It reiterated Japan’s long-standing position that peace and stability across the Taiwan Strait are indispensable to Japan’s security and to the stability of the international community.
The report argued that China’s growing military reach is reinforced by closer operational coordination with Russia.
For the first time, the Ministry of Defense’s public digest contained a dedicated section illustrating the evolution of China-Russia military cooperation, including joint naval exercises, long-range bomber patrols, coordinated naval operations, and participation in each other’s military exercises. The report said that the scale, frequency and geographic scope of these activities have continued to expand.
On a related note, the report reflects Tokyo’s growing concern that security developments in Europe and the Indo-Pacific can no longer be viewed separately.
Regarding North Korea, the white paper stated that Pyongyang has continued providing Russia with ballistic missiles, artillery ammunition, and other military equipment since 2023, while North Korean troops have participated in combat operations following their deployment to Russia.
It warned that expanding Russia-North Korea military cooperation could strengthen North Korea’s military capabilities over the medium to long term.
The white paper said that North Korean forces could gain valuable battlefield experience from the war in Ukraine. The ministry does not currently assess that Russian assistance has already strengthened North Korea’s military capabilities, but warned that continued cooperation could eventually lead to technology transfers and improvements in Pyongyang’s military strength.
One of the most notable additions to this year’s white paper is a new section examining what it called the “new way of warfare.” Drawing lessons from the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, the report highlighted the growing role of drones, artificial intelligence, and adequate stockpiles in future warfare.
It also stressed the importance of sustaining combat operations during prolonged conflicts.
Reflecting those lessons, the white paper elevated the section on Japan’s defense production and technological base from a chapter to a full part of the report, underscoring its growing importance to national defense. It also referred to the easing of Japan’s defense equipment export rules earlier this year, arguing that defense exports can strengthen the deterrence capabilities of partner countries while helping build an environment for mutual support among allies and like-minded nations. 
Taken together, the 2026 white paper portrayed China’s expanding military reach into the Pacific as the defining feature of Japan’s security environment. Japan must respond, the report argued, not only through higher defense spending, but also by strengthening alliances, its defense industrial base, and preparations for a new era of warfare.

articles.title: Malaysia’s DAP to Hold Vote on Whether to Remain in Anwar’s ‘Unity’ Government
articles.full_text:
The announcement follows the Pakatan Harapan coalition’s bruising defeat in the Negeri Sembilan state election on Saturday.
Anthony Loke, the secretary-general of Malaysia’s Democratic Action Party (DAP), attends a state election campaign event in Yong Peng, Johor State, Malaysia, July 3, 2026.
Malaysia’s Democratic Action Party (DAP) will soon decide whether to remain in Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s “unity” government, after performing poorly in a string of state elections.
The DAP, which is currently the largest party in Anwar’s Pakatan Harapan (PH) coalition, holding 40 of its 77 seats in the federal parliament, has been hemorrhaging support due to the government’s perceived mishandling of corruption cases and concerns over its commitment to promised reforms.
In a press conference today, the DAP’s Secretary-General Anthony Loke said that the party’s central executive committee (CEC) had decided to convene a special national congress on August 16, at which it would table a motion on whether the party should remain a part of Anwar’s administration.
He said that about 4,000 DAP delegates would be given the right to decide the party’s position. “The decision will be made by the delegates, not the CEC. We will leave it to their wisdom,” Loke said, as per local media. DAP currently has five ministers and ​seven deputy ministers ​in Anwar’s cabinet.
The announcement comes after PH was trounced in a state election in Negeri Sembilan on Saturday, when the coalition won just 11 of the 36 seats in the legislative assembly, down from 17 previously. The election was won by an alliance of Barisan Nasional (BN), PH’s partner at the federal level, and the pan-Malay Perikatan Nasional (PN) coalition, which collectively won 25 seats. Loke, who currently serves as minister of transport, lost his seat in the state legislative assembly, a position he had held for 13 years, prompting him to resign his post as the DAP’s chairman for Negeri Sembilan.
This follows similar losses that Anwar’s coalition suffered in Johor last month and Sabah in November. While the DAP did not perform terribly in Negeri Sembilan – the party won nine of the 11 seats that it contested – it suffered more grievous setbacks in Johor and Sabah, as its predominantly urban Chinese voter base abstained or switched to other parties.
The DAP, which has traditionally been associated with Malaysia’s ethnic Chinese minority but also attracts liberal and reformist voters of all races, has been impacted by the growing disillusionment with Anwar and PH. This crested last year following a string of corruption scandals, including reports of widespread misconduct at the Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission. These have tarnished Anwar’s anti-corruption credentials and stirred up discontent among progressive supporters who since 2022 have grown frustrated with the slow implementation of promised reforms.
In March, DAP announced that it ​would “evaluate its position” in the governing coalition for the next general election, due to its disappointment with the government’s approach to corruption and the difficulty of being forced to defend the compromises made by PH after striking an unlikely alliance with BN after the general election of 2022.
In any event, the result in Negeri Sembilan has raised questions about the future of the DAP, with some Malaysian analysts suggesting that Loke, who has generally been known as a pragmatist who is willing to play the coalition game, could be challenged or eclipsed by more assertive reformists within the party.
DAP national Chairman Gobind Singh Deo said on Sunday that the party accepted the result in Negeri Sembilan “with full humility,” the South China Morning Post reported.
“The message from the electorate is clear,” he said. “We must and will undertake a thorough assessment of the outcome, listen carefully to the concerns of the people, and work hard to regain their confidence and support.”
While the DAP says that it will continue to support PH, its defection would obviously further complicate Anwar’s political position, which is under threat from an incipient pan-Malay pact between BN and PN. As I noted yesterday, Saturday’s election in Negeri Sembilan witnessed close cooperation between the two coalitions, particularly between two of their largest respective constituent parties, the United Malays National Organization (UMNO) and the Islamist PAS.
If it holds and coheres, this alliance could prove decisive at the next general election, which must be held by early 2028, but could be called earlier. Anwar has previously said that he may call a snap election if the tensions between PH and BN, which remain federal partners even as they engage in bruising contests at the state level, becomes too difficult to manage.
Malaysia’s Democratic Action Party (DAP) will soon decide whether to remain in Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s “unity” government, after performing poorly in a string of state elections.
The DAP, which is currently the largest party in Anwar’s Pakatan Harapan (PH) coalition, holding 40 of its 77 seats in the federal parliament, has been hemorrhaging support due to the government’s perceived mishandling of corruption cases and concerns over its commitment to promised reforms.
In a press conference today, the DAP’s Secretary-General Anthony Loke said that the party’s central executive committee (CEC) had decided to convene a special national congress on August 16, at which it would table a motion on whether the party should remain a part of Anwar’s administration.
He said that about 4,000 DAP delegates would be given the right to decide the party’s position. “The decision will be made by the delegates, not the CEC. We will leave it to their wisdom,” Loke said, as per local media. DAP currently has five ministers and ​seven deputy ministers ​in Anwar’s cabinet.
The announcement comes after PH was trounced in a state election in Negeri Sembilan on Saturday, when the coalition won just 11 of the 36 seats in the legislative assembly, down from 17 previously. The election was won by an alliance of Barisan Nasional (BN), PH’s partner at the federal level, and the pan-Malay Perikatan Nasional (PN) coalition, which collectively won 25 seats. Loke, who currently serves as minister of transport, lost his seat in the state legislative assembly, a position he had held for 13 years, prompting him to resign his post as the DAP’s chairman for Negeri Sembilan.
This follows similar losses that Anwar’s coalition suffered in Johor last month and Sabah in November. While the DAP did not perform terribly in Negeri Sembilan – the party won nine of the 11 seats that it contested – it suffered more grievous setbacks in Johor and Sabah, as its predominantly urban Chinese voter base abstained or switched to other parties.
The DAP, which has traditionally been associated with Malaysia’s ethnic Chinese minority but also attracts liberal and reformist voters of all races, has been impacted by the growing disillusionment with Anwar and PH. These have tarnished Anwar’s anti-corruption credentials and stirred up discontent among progressive supporters who since 2022 have grown frustrated with the slow implementation of promised reforms.

In any event, the result in Negeri Sembilan has raised questions about the future of the DAP, with some Malaysian analysts suggesting that Loke, who has generally been known as a pragmatist who is willing to play the coalition game, could be challenged or eclipsed by more assertive reformists within the party.
DAP national Chairman Gobind Singh Deo said on Sunday that the party accepted the result in Negeri Sembilan “with full humility,” the South China Morning Post reported.

While the DAP says that it will continue to support PH, its defection would obviously further complicate Anwar’s political position, which is under threat from an incipient pan-Malay pact between BN and PN. As I noted yesterday, Saturday’s election in Negeri Sembilan witnessed close cooperation between the two coalitions, particularly between two of their largest respective constituent parties, the United Malays National Organization (UMNO) and the Islamist PAS.
If it holds and coheres, this alliance could prove decisive at the next general election, which must be held by early 2028, but could be called earlier. articles.title: Iran in Port Sudan? The Next Threat to Asian Markets
articles.full_text:
The Red Sea corridor Asian trade depends on has another volatile shore, and almost nobody is watching it.
Container lines began testing a return to the Suez route in early 2026, with the first Asia to Europe services shifting back to Red Sea sailings from mid-February on the condition that security conditions held. That condition is generally read as a question about Yemen. It is at least as much a question about the western shore of the same corridor, where a four-year war has left roughly 700 kilometers of Sudanese coastline under a government that depends on foreign weapons suppliers, principally Iran, Turkey, Russia and China, and that has been willing to discuss access to its ports as part of the price.
Port Sudan has been the seat of that government since Khartoum fell out of its hands in 2023, which makes the coast the asset that keeps the authorities supplied, solvent and diplomatically visible. It is therefore the asset most available for trade. Sudan’s frontage sits north of the Bab al-Mandab strait, along the stretch of water vessels enter after they consider themselves clear of the Yemeni threat envelope.
The Iranian supply relationship is documented, not merely inferred. Tehran and Khartoum restored diplomatic relations in October 2023, and in April 2026 the United States Department of Justice charged an Iranian national in Los Angeles with brokering it, describing a contract worth more than seventy million dollars for Mohajer-6 drones from Iran’s defense ministry to Sudan’s military, a letter of intent to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps for bomb fuses, and payments routed through an Oman-registered company.
The traffic runs both ways, which is where the monitoring case becomes concrete. The United Nations Panel of Experts on Yemen has documented a smuggling network operating between Yemeni and Sudanese territory since 2023. Its final report of October 2025 describes the Houthis as the principal controllers of regional smuggling as interdiction tightened in the Arabian Sea. Analysts at the Italian Institute for International Political Studies, drawing on that reporting, identify a route between Port Sudan and Al Salif in Hodeidah governorate for weapons and personnel, and note Yemeni coast guard interceptions of shipments out of Sudan during 2025. Their own assessment is that indications of cooperation are growing while conclusive evidence lags. That gap is the point.
What Tehran wants in return remains contested. In March 2024 the Wall Street Journal reported that Iran had sought a permanent naval facility on the coast and been refused, an account both governments denied. In December 2025 the same newspaper reported that Port Sudan had offered Russia a twenty-five year arrangement covering up to three hundred personnel and four warships, prompting a warning from Washington. The pattern matters more than any single transaction. Coastal access is the currency a besieged government spends when its need for weapons outruns its ability to pay.
None of this requires a view on which belligerent deserves to prevail, and none of it requires Port Sudan to become a firing position. A government living off its own harbor has little incentive to make that harbor unusable, and the near-term risk lies in transfer, resupply and berthing rather than launch. The Yemeni precedent is instructive precisely because it shows how the first category converts into the second. At the latitude of Port Sudan the main shipping lane runs roughly 150 kilometers offshore, inside the reach of systems Iran already exports, and a threat from that shore would sit north of Bab al-Mandab, in the half of the run carriers currently treat as safe. Underwriters price passages rather than individual coastlines. A corridor with two contested shores is one insurers have little reason to reopen.
The exposure is disproportionately Asian. Around twenty-two percent of global seaborne container trade moved through the Suez Canal in 2023, according to UN Trade and Development, most of it on lanes connecting East and South Asia to Europe. By May 2025 transits were running roughly seventy percent below their 2023 average, as recorded in the agency’s Review of Maritime Transport, with the Cape diversion adding ten to fifteen days to those voyages. Chinese, Indian, Japanese and South Korean shippers carried the largest share of the cost. Singapore, Port Klang and Colombo absorbed the network effects.
The monitoring architecture is not built for any of this. The Security Council’s Sudan arms embargo under resolution 1591 applies to Darfur, a mandate written in 2005 for a land war in the west, so the Panel of Experts reports on a theatre that excludes the coastline where the consequential transfers arrive. Twenty-one years on, that geography has never been updated to match the war being fought. Extending the scope of investigation nationally is the clean fix; tasking the Panel to report on maritime and aviation movements into Port Sudan is the minimum. A second gap sits alongside it, since two Panels of Experts examine opposite shores of the same water under separate mandates with no requirement to reconcile findings, which leaves a route from Port Sudan to Al Salif falling between them.
Even the machinery that exists has been allowed to stall. Under resolution 2772 of 2025 the Council extended the Sudan Panel yet could not agree on its composition, so the Panel went unconstituted, missing both its interim report due that August and its mandated quarterly updates. Algeria objected to the expert nominated to cover armed groups. China and Pakistan objected to the expert nominated to cover arms. The renewal that followed in September was a technical rollover, with members divided over whether to reference Sudan’s worsening situation at all. Monitoring capacity is not scarce here. It is being withheld, and the seat covering arms is the one that proved hardest to fill.
The remedies are unglamorous and already available. Satellite radar and automatic identification system gap analysis run commercially along the Sudanese and Eritrean coasts. Port state control inspections and manifest scrutiny at transhipment hubs raise the cost of a route without anyone interdicting at sea. The Los Angeles prosecution worked because financial intelligence connected a shell company, global banking channels and informal value transfer into a single case file.
The UN watches the Yemeni shore because ships were attacked from it, and does not watch the Sudanese shore because nothing has been attacked from it yet, excluding of course untold scores of Sudanese civilians by the arms flowing there. Monitoring built on that logic arrives one crisis late, every time. The states with the most to lose economically are the ones furthest from the conflict, and monitoring is cheap set against a second rerouting of Asia to Europe trade. Whether the Red Sea ends this decade with one contested shore or two is being decided now, in a conflict most of the exposed states have chosen not to engage.

articles.title: It’s Time for the East Asia Summit to Tackle Nuclear Proliferation
articles.full_text:
As more countries consider acquiring nuclear weapons, the EAS should take the lead in addressing the growing challenges of proliferation.
Officials attend the East Asia Summit Preparatory Senior Officials’ Meeting in Port Dickson, Malaysia, Sep. 10, 2025.
In 1963, U.S. President John F. Kennedy warned that in the 1970s the world might have up to 25 nuclear weapon states. He was making the case for an international agreement to limit the proliferation of nuclear weapons. That agreement, the NPT, proved to be perhaps the most significant arms control agreement ever negotiated.
Today we stand at a similar juncture. Left unattended the risk of nuclear weapons proliferation is significant and growing; nowhere more so than in the Indo-Pacific.
The NPT succeeded because it convinced countries contemplating acquiring nuclear weapons that proliferation was ultimately destabilizing. It rested on a series of incentives such as access to nuclear power for peaceful purposes; an international safeguards regime, which engendered confidence that nuclear material was not diverted from peaceful to military purposes; and the pledge that ultimately the five nuclear weapon states recognized by the treaty would engage in comprehensive disarmament. Not every element of this compact was delivered but enough was to convince most countries not to consider crossing the nuclear threshold.
Those assumptions are now being revisited. Countries such as South Korea and Poland talk openly about acquiring nuclear weapons. Others are revisiting whether it is an option they should keep open. Even in Australia, a leading advocate for non-proliferation, some 39 percent of Australians support acquiring nuclear weapons, according to the latest Lowy Institute poll. The dominoes are upright for now, but if one falls others will surely follow.
At the heart of the proliferation challenge are shifting perceptions of how to buttress security in a world facing a bonfire of certainties.
What we are seeing in the Indo-Pacific is a double hedging strategy. Regional states want to hedge against China’s hegemonic ambitions. But they also want to hedge against U.S. unreliability, which has been President Donald Trump’s legacy to Asia, Europe, and elsewhere.
This has significant implications for extended nuclear deterrence, one of the supporting pillars of the nuclear non-proliferation regime. If the United States is perceived as an unreliable partner, how credible is extended nuclear deterrence? Can we really believe, for example, the U.S. would sacrifice San Francisco to save Sydney? 
The end of the post-war international order is leading more countries to invest in deterrent capabilities and to pursue a larger measure of strategic autonomy. These are seen as buffers against strategic instability and an overreliance on the U.S. cavalry coming to the assistance of its allies and partners.
For some the logic of both deterrence and strategic autonomy ends with nuclear weapons, increasingly seen as both the ultimate deterrent and the ultimate protector of autonomy. Nuclear arms are the reason, some argue, why North Korea (which withdrew from the NPT) has not been attacked while NPT member Iran has; why Ukraine would have been better off if it had retained Soviet era nuclear weapons.
These assumptions may be questionable, even simplistic, but they are gaining more traction. They cannot be ignored.
If we want to prevent the superficially appealing from becoming compelling, we need a more open discussion about both the strategic anxieties behind an interest in nuclear weapons and the risks of nuclear weapons proliferation. It is a discussion that may require a vocabulary quite different to the grammar of the NPT and the routine stalemate of successive NPT Review conferences.
How best to structure such a dialogue? Track II engagement can be useful, but these are issues that need to be addressed at the government level and in a multilateral context.
In the Indo-Pacific the weakening of regional institutions does not help. But could this be a topic on which agreement on a dialogue may be relatively easy to secure in a body such as the East Asia Summit (EAS). The China-U.S. faultline and the U.S. loss of faith in multilateralism has steadily neutered the EAS, as they have other Indo-Pacific regional arrangements. But non-proliferation is an issue that should transcend such divisions.
The United States, China, and Russia may not welcome a discussion on the causes of contemporary strategic anxiety, but none has an interest in the proliferation of nuclear weapons, just as the U.S. and the Soviet Union were on a non-proliferation unity ticket during the Cold War. And even those EAS members who may be flirting with the idea of acquiring nuclear weapons should have no fundamental objection to putting in place a structured dialogue to address the challenges of nuclear weapons proliferation. It commits them only to a deeper understanding of the underlying issues.
Australia – which has been at the center of multilateral diplomacy on nuclear non-proliferation, from the strengthening of IAEA safeguards to the negotiations on the Comprehensive Test Ban treaty, all the NPT Review conferences, and the negotiation of the South Pacific Nuclear Free Zone Treaty – could take a lead in brokering such a dialogue. Even better, it could be a joint initiative of Australia and ASEAN, which would give it real weight.
Such a dialogue, nested in the architecture of the EAS, might critically examine the assumption that acquiring a nuclear weapon strengthens a country’s security. It could examine the huge cost of a nuclear weapons program, as well as the technical complexity. In short, it could serve to demonstrate that the case for nuclear weapons may not be as straightforward as some think. At the very least, such a dialogue may encourage would-be proliferators to recognize that easy answers to complex questions may not be in their long-term security interests.
An EAS dialogue on nuclear non-proliferation may also offer some hope that regional institutions can move beyond life support. It is true that the high point of multilateralism is behind us. But for all the emphasis on sovereignty, self-reliance, and putting national interests first, we are still left with the reality that some issues can only be resolved through multilateral cooperation. 
No amount of chest thumping can alter the simple truth that problems without borders do not disappear with the abandonment of multilateralism. They just need to be addressed in a different way. And if they are not, we will all be both poorer and less secure.
This essay was first published in the Asian Peace Programme (APP) web page. The APP is housed in the National University of Singapore (NUS).

articles.title: What Philippine President Marcos Said About China in His State of the Nation Address
articles.full_text:
His rhetoric was familiar, but carried additional weight in light of recent clashes between Chinese and Philippine vessels in the South China Sea.
Philippine lawmakers applaud while President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. delivers his State of the Nation Address at the Philippine Congress in Quezon City, July 27, 2026.
Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. ended his fifth State of the Nation Address on July 27 by making veiled remarks directed at China as he enjoined Filipinos to unite and defend the country’s honor.
Marcos mentioned China only once in his speech when he enumerated the countries that provided oil supply after the closure of the Strait of Hormuz in March and April. But the last part of his speech alluded to the country’s defensive posture in the West Philippine Sea, even if he did not directly name China.
Marcos addressed both “friends” and “detractors” when he called Filipinos a “noble, kind, gracious, and great race.” He added: “We are not greedy. We are not racists. We are not liars.” He was obviously referring to the controversial animated video released by a Chinese state media outlet depicting Filipinos as monkeys.
He asserted that Filipinos “do not yield” which was a reiteration of his speech in 2024 in Singapore pertaining to the country’s defense of its maritime zones. He made it clear that this was about upholding the 2016 ruling of the Permanent Court of Arbitration, which invalidated China’s “nine-dash line” claim over most parts of the South China Sea and affirmed the Philippines’ sovereignty over features lying within its exclusive economic zone (EEZ) and continental shelf.
Marcos acknowledged the 10th anniversary of the Arbitral Award and underscored the support received by the Philippines from various governments. “This is not a claim that we advance alone, nor is it one that we will abandon,” he said.
He added that his government will push back against any domestic or foreign attempt to undermine the Award, which addressed China’s continuing insistence that the decision is illegal, null, void, and has no binding effect.
This rhetoric is not new but it carried more weight in light of recent clashes involving Chinese and Philippine ships at Second Thomas Shoal (known in the Philippines as Ayungin Shoal), which is claimed by the two countries despite being located inside Manila’s EEZ.
The incident was tackled during a meeting between Marcos and the Chinese Ambassador a week before the State of the Nation Address. But it didn’t ease the verbal spat among some Chinese and Filipino officials. It even prompted the Philippines’ Defense Secretary to accuse the Chinese diplomat of violating an agreement about embargoing the contents of the conversation during the meeting. The Defense Secretary also called for the resignation of “pro-China” politicians who reject or refuse to uphold the laws affirming the country’s sovereignty over the West Philippine Sea.
The appeal to nationalism was triggered by Marcos, who ended his annual speech before the joint session of Congress by rephrasing the country’s national anthem. “We will not be subdued by those who seek to oppress us,” he said.
Marcos invoked the lessons of history to remind Filipinos of the struggle for independence and the need to rally behind the government’s position in resolving the maritime tension with China. But Marcos didn’t point out that if history is to be used as reference, the country’s resistance against foreign oppressors was about ending the colonial rule of the United States and Japan during the first half of the 20th century. This is quite ironic since the two countries are now the strongest allies of the Philippine government in calling out China’s aggressive actions in the West Philippine Sea.
Marcos articulated the priorities of his administration but his speech was also significant for what he didn’t say. For example, he made no reference to the ongoing impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte even if it was reported later that he approved the release of tax and bank records of his erstwhile political ally. In the case of China, Marcos only mentioned the country’s big neighbor once, but he devoted the last part of his speech to highlighting the maritime dispute and tension over the West Philippine Sea not just to affirm his foreign policy but also to appeal for unity amid the intensifying political crisis and continuing public outrage over the failure to end corruption and ease the economic hardships of the people.

The appeal to nationalism was triggered by Marcos, who ended his annual speech before the joint session of Congress by rephrasing the country’s national anthem. “We will not be subdued by those who seek to oppress us,” he said.
Marcos invoked the lessons of history to remind Filipinos of the struggle for independence and the need to rally behind the government’s position in resolving the maritime tension with China. But Marcos didn’t point out that if history is to be used as reference, the country’s resistance against foreign oppressors was about ending the colonial rule of the United States and Japan during the first half of the 20th century. This is quite ironic since the two countries are now the strongest allies of the Philippine government in calling out China’s aggressive actions in the West Philippine Sea.
Marcos articulated the priorities of his administration but his speech was also significant for what he didn’t say. For example, he made no reference to the ongoing impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte even if it was reported later that he approved the release of tax and bank records of his erstwhile political ally. In the case of China, Marcos only mentioned the country’s big neighbor once, but he devoted the last part of his speech to highlighting the maritime dispute and tension over the West Philippine Sea not just to affirm his foreign policy but also to appeal for unity amid the intensifying political crisis and continuing public outrage over the failure to end corruption and ease the economic hardships of the people.
Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. ended his fifth State of the Nation Address on July 27 by making veiled remarks directed at China as he enjoined Filipinos to unite and defend the country’s honor.
Marcos mentioned China only once in his speech when he enumerated the countries that provided oil supply after the closure of the Strait of Hormuz in March and April. But the last part of his speech alluded to the country’s defensive posture in the West Philippine Sea, even if he did not directly name China.
Mong Palatino served for two terms in the House of Representatives in the Philippines representing the youth sector.
articles.summary: His rhetoric was familiar, but carried additional weight in light of recent clashes between Chinese and Philippine vessels in the South China Sea.

articles.title: Donald Trump’s Tariff Re-Do in Southeast Asia
articles.full_text:
The capricious treatment of partners and allies threatens to do long-term damage to Washington’s standing in the region.
U.S. President Donald Trump exits the stage after delivering remarks at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, Jan. 21, 2026.
Last year, the United States imposed sweeping tariffs on its trade partners worldwide, including those in Southeast Asia. The tariffs, which went as high as 49 percent, were based largely on the size of each country’s bilateral trade surplus with the United States. Really big exporters, like Thailand and Vietnam, faced stiff tariffs.
Indonesia and Malaysia quickly agreed to lopsided reciprocal trade agreements with the U.S. to get the tariffs lowered to under 20 percent. That may have been hasty as the deals contain numerous provisions that are seemingly impossible to enforce.  In any case, the U.S. Supreme Court struck down the tariffs in February.
Trump’s love of tariffs has not been deterred, however, and the administration soon launched a wave of investigations under the authority of Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. This gives the U.S. Trade Representative broad powers to impose tariffs if they conclude that trade partners are engaging in unfair practices or using forced labor. The results are in on the forced labor probe, and the administration has concluded that 60 countries are in violation of Section 301. Those found to be in violation are subject to new tariffs of between 10 and 12.5 percent.
Singapore, Vietnam, and Thailand are among those being tariffed at the higher rate. Indonesia and Malaysia, which have conveniently already signed reciprocal trade agreements with the U.S., are subject to the lower 10 percent rate. Of course, the official explanation is not being received well. Singapore’s Foreign Minister Vivian Balakrishnan noted that there was “no technical or economic basis” for the tariffs, and that the U.S. actually runs a trade surplus with Singapore.
One could be forgiven for thinking the new round of Section 301 investigations is merely a thin pretext for re-tariffing trade partners after the first round of tariffs were struck down by the Supreme Court. But the Singapore case is worth unpacking, as it underscores just how complex international trade and investment networks are and the extent to which the new round of tariffs seems to miss the point entirely.
In April 2025, Singapore was hit with a 10 percent tariff by the Trump Administration. This was relatively light, compared to higher punitive tariffs levied on countries like Thailand and Vietnam that run large bilateral trade surpluses with the United States. Singapore’s new 12.5 percent tariff under Section 301 is therefore higher than the previous one. It is even more peculiar because Singapore runs a trade deficit with the U.S., meaning Singapore imports more goods and services from the U.S. than it exports, which is precisely what the U.S. claimed it wanted in the first place.
Singapore’s total exports of goods to the U.S., including re-exported goods, reached $54 billion in 2025 (at current exchange rates). During that same time period, Singapore imported from the U.S. $54.6 billion worth of goods. That means they ran a slight deficit in tradable goods. When you add services to the calculation, the deficit widens considerably. In 2025, Singapore imported $95 billion worth of services from American firms, while exporting just $50 billion. This means Singapore is actually running a total trade deficit with the United States of about $45.5 billion.
The Trump administration is tariffing a long-time ally that runs a large bilateral trade deficit with the United States, something the administration claims it wants countries to do more of. Beyond trade, Singapore is also a crucial destination for U.S. investment in the region. American investors and firms like to set up entities in Singapore because of its strong governance system and attractive tax rates. They then use it as an entry point for reinvesting around the region. As of 2024, the cumulative stock of U.S. direct investment in Singapore was recorded at $608 billion.
Trump’s first attempt to tariff the region was knocked down by the Supreme Court, but not before several countries signed lopsided trade agreements. Those that didn’t, like Singapore, are now being hit with a second wave of tariffs using rather thin justifications under Section 301. The new tariffs seemingly ignore the fact that Singapore has a bilateral trade deficit with the United States, and also serves as a key entry point for U.S. investment in the region.
At this point we have become largely inured to the vagaries of trade policy in the Trump administration. But at some point, one has to believe that long-time allies and the networks of trade and investment that flow through them and which have historically benefited the U.S. are going to be permanently undermined and damaged the longer they are subjected to such whimsical policy-making. And it may not be easy to reconstruct them in the future.

articles.title: Myanmar’s Detained Leader Aung San Suu Kyi Meets Red Cross Official
articles.full_text:
The move is intended to weaken ASEAN’s determination to hold Myanmar to the Five-Point Consensus and widen the divisions between the bloc’s member states.
Myanmar’s detained former leader Aung San Suu Kyi shakes hands with Arnaud de Baecque, resident representative of the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) to Myanmar, in Naypyidaw, Aug. 3, 2026.
Myanmar’s detained former leader Aung San Suu Kyi met yesterday with a representative of the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), as coup leader-turned-president Min Aung Hlaing prepares to visit Thailand.
The military-backed government yesterday released four photos of the 81-year-old meeting with an ICRC official, whom a government spokesperson identified as Arnaud de Baecque, the ICRC’s resident representative in Myanmar.
The ICRC confirmed the meeting, stating that the visit was carried out in accordance with the organization’s standards and procedures for visiting people deprived of liberty. This “included the opportunity to speak with Daw Aung San Suu Kyi in private,” it stated.
“In line with the ICRC’s working methods, detention visits provide people deprived of liberty with the opportunity to exchange news with their families,” it added. The ICRC did not reveal any details of what was discussed, but said that “observations and recommendations related to the visit are shared exclusively and confidentially with the detaining authorities.”
In one of the photographs, Suu Kyi is seen shaking hands with de Baecque and sitting with him in a bare wood-paneled room with parquet floors, containing only two chairs and a coffee table. Another shows the deposed leader in another room cutting a birthday cake inscribed with the message “Happy Birthday Aunty Suu 19.6.2026.”
These images are among just a handful that the military has released of Suu Kyi since she was removed from power in a military coup on February 1, 2021, just hours before she was due to be sworn in for a second term as Myanmar’s de facto leader. Since then, she has been in the military’s custody and is currently serving a lengthy prison term on a range of far-fetched charges, including incitement, corruption, election fraud, and violation of Myanmar’s Official Secrets Act.
Suu Kyi’s meeting with the ICRC representative comes amid a push by the new military-backed government to normalize its relations with ASEAN and other important partners. In May, the authorities announced her relocation from prison to house arrest, alongside a broader amnesty of political prisoners.
However, despite the release of one photo of Suu Kyi at the time, and assurances from Naypyidaw that she was in good health, many were skeptical. Suu Kyi’s son Kim Aris launched a “proof of life” campaign, demanding more substantial evidence of her health and physical condition, and there was growing international pressure, including from ASEAN, for access to the detained leader.
Aris said in a statement that he welcomed the ICRC visit, which he described as “the first positive development” concerning his mother for more than five years. Although it was an important first step, he said, “it must not be the last.”
“I hope this leads to further humanitarian progress, including direct contact with my mother, access for our family, credible and independently verified information about her wellbeing, and ultimately her immediate and unconditional release, together with all political prisoners,” he said.
The Assistance Association for Political Prisoners likewise described the meeting as a “partial victory driven by collective pressure from domestic and international organizations,” including ASEAN, but said that Suu Kyi should be released immediately. “The military’s decision to permit access solely to the ICRC makes it very clear that she remains a prisoner,” it stated. (A Myanmar propaganda account on X made this point clear yesterday.)
The timing and nature of the meeting are clearly intentional. Since assuming the office of president in April, Min Aung Hlaing has pushed hard for Myanmar’s reintegration into ASEAN. The 11-nation bloc has barred Myanmar from its summits since late 2021, over its failure to implement its Five-Point Consensus plan for resolving the country’s post-coup conflict, which involved pledges to cease violence, allow humanitarian access, and engage in political dialogue involving “all parties” to the country’s conflict.
Min Aung Hlaing is set to visit Thailand this week, where he will no doubt seek to advance efforts at normalization. Over the past two years, Thailand has been a strong advocate of bringing Myanmar back into the “ASEAN family,” and helped broker an informal meeting between ASEAN’s foreign ministers and Myanmar Foreign Minister Tin Maung Swe in Bangkok on July 12.
Sure enough, Thai Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow said in a statement yesterday that he welcomed reports of the meeting and expressed “hope that the Government of Myanmar will undertake further positive steps towards lasting peace and stability in Myanmar.” In comments to the Straits Times, he added that the authorities in Myanmar “seem to be listening to our repeated urging that we need more positive developments on the Lady,” as Suu Kyi is known to many within Myanmar. He added, “It’s their way of responding to our concerns.”
At the same time, however, Min Aung Hlaing has shown few signs that he is willing to make concessions. In a speech to parliament last week, he rejected ASEAN’s Five-Point Consensus, which the military-proxy parliament last month denounced as an unwarranted interference in Myanmar’s internal affairs. In early July, Myanmar’s government rejected a request by the current ASEAN special envoy, Philippine Foreign Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro, for “brief access” to Suu Kyi.
In this context, providing limited access to the detained leader, albeit in a form that underlines her status as a prisoner, is a cost-free move intended to weaken ASEAN’s resolve to hold Myanmar to the Five-Point Consensus and widen the divisions between the bloc’s member states.
The Myanmar military has long been aware of the potent symbolic power of Aung San Suu Kyi, and the ability to leverage this to its own advantage. In 2017, I argued that while the totemic Nobel laureate “was effective in rallying international opposition to Myanmar’s ruling generals, it also gave the latter an easy route back to legitimacy.”
This small step will do nothing to shift the positions of the Western governments that have been most critical of Myanmar’s military since the coup. It is also unlikely to be enough to gain readmission to ASEAN, at least for now. Lazaro said last month that Myanmar’s full reintegration was “still far off” due to its lack of compliance with the Five-Point Consensus, and the bloc will clearly need to take a significant step in this direction if Myanmar is to fill its seat at the bloc’s next summit in November.
But it does have the potential to erode ASEAN’s position, and prod dissenting member states further into the pro-engagement camp. It buys the military time to weaken and divide those resisting its rule, with the eye to a possible normalization further down the line, perhaps in 2028, when Thailand will assume ASEAN’s rotating chairmanship.
For now, Min Aung Hlaing and his cronies are engaged in a game of seeing just how low they can set the bar.

articles.title: Why India’s Cockroach Movement Might Not Collapse Like the Others
articles.full_text:
The Cockroach Janta Party reflects every hallmark of modern decentralized leadership theories, but is set to leave a lasting imprint on Indian politics.
People gather during a protest organized by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) at Jantar Mantar in New Delhi, India, demanding accountability over alleged examination irregularities and education reforms, July 19, 2026.
When Indian Supreme Court Justice Surya Kant compared certain unemployed youth and activists to cockroaches and parasites in May, he gave a generation searching for a shared identity the charge required to build one. Within days that slur became a rallying cry. Millions of young Indians declared “Main Bhi Cockroach” (‘I too am a cockroach’), turned the insult into memes, and launched a political party in the same breath.
Some framed this as Prime Minister Narendra Modi misreading the political environment – after all, his own government gave India’s marginalized and unemployed youth the spark they needed to organize. But that top-down classic political framing overlooks emerging leadership theories, the mechanics of peer-to-peer digital communication, and global trends already underway. Gen Z uprisings had toppled or shaken governments in Nepal, Bangladesh, Kenya, and Madagascar over the previous two years. And each one built from the same digital scaffolding comprised of user digital trace creation, reproduction, and platform scalability.
India’s administration either assumed it was immune from that global pattern or lacked the tools to recognize the trend at all. The failure, then, was its blindness to a new form of political organizing.
The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) reflects every hallmark of modern decentralized leadership theories. Digital traces left by one user become stimuli that guide the next user, producing coordination without any central command. Three more granular properties define this process: independent individual acts, reproducibility by peers who copy and adapt what they see, and platform architectures that scale those traces far beyond the original digital trace and network. The CJP displayed all three within its first week of existence.
Its origins trace back to urban, globally educated, and digitally native figures – the same traits seen in other Gen Z-led movements. Abhijeet Dipke, who holds a master’s in public relations from Boston University, founded the “party” through a simple website and sign-up form built around a short, provocative question he posted online. He then built the CJP’s manifesto and branding using AI. 
Saurav Das, a New Delhi-based investigative journalist who began filing Right to Information requests at 18, became the movement’s public voice, using digital media updates to amplify protest messaging. Sign-ups  passed 100,000 within two days and reached 350,000 soon after. The party’s social media followers climbed toward 18 million in a few days, briefly outpacing the official accounts of both Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and Congress.
The “cockroach” movement grew exponentially in a short period, like similar movements across the globe, because it tapped into deep grievances among a significant share of the country’s native digital society. India’s Periodic Labor Force Survey put unemployment among those aged 15 to 29 at 15.2 percent in March 2026, against 3 to 5.6 percent overall. Azim Premji University estimated more than 40 percent of college graduates under 25 were unemployed, roughly 11 million people. 
The cancellation of a medical entrance exam, the National Eligibility cum Entrance Test, following leak allegations turned an abstract grievance into an immediate one. 2.3 million exam-registered students saw themselves losing a concrete shot at a government-recognized medical career.
Education and employment failures function as fertile ground for collective meaning making because they touch nearly every young household, regardless of religion or caste. That is why the movement drew Hindu and Muslim families to pray and eat side by side at protest sites, with a Muslim cook feeding demonstrators daily and Sikh gurdwaras running community kitchens.
Online, the movement leverages memes as its central mode of communication and dissemination. Memes carry a distinct advantage over other digital objects. They can be created in seconds, convey essential information creatively, and let any user grasp the core message quickly and playfully. Memes are also powerful because their format invites recreation. A user does not simply view a meme and move on. They copy its structure, replace its content, and repost it, multiplying the original trace across many variations.
Declaration memes, campaign poster parodies, exam leak satire reels, and crocodile versus cockroach power imbalance imagery each carry their own function. Each variation modifies the shared digital environment further, prompting the next round of recreation. Once this accumulation crosses a threshold, an autonomous individual act converts into cumulative and scalable collective coordination. 
Kant’s original insult itself, it could be argued, functioned as that threshold trace. It carried enough affective charge, given existing grievances around unemployment and exam integrity, to convert millions of isolated frustrations into a shared, recognizable identity within days.
Some national observers are skeptical that a movement built on emotional reaction and algorithmic amplification can last. I would argue otherwise. The CJP stands a stronger chance of durable success than most of its counterparts for one specific reason. 
Toppling a government is easier than building institutions capable of governing afterward. For example, Nepal’s 2006 revolution overthrew a monarchy only to produce 17 successive governments and prolonged economic stagnation. More recent examples in both Nepal and Bangladesh have shown that digital coordination excels at government disruption and struggles with construction. The viral architecture that spreads outrage rarely contains the sustained negotiation, expertise, and trust that governing requires. 
The CJP, however, seems to have decisively moved past that bottleneck by converting a meme into a formal political party. This single, early strategic step pushed the movement beyond the confines of digital virality, providing a path for translating grievance into concrete and actionable policy demands through institutional means. In addition, its structure gives the CJP an organizational depth most leaderless uprisings never develop. The movement also enjoys a form of legitimacy rare among comparable cases. It draws support across religious lines, from opposition politicians and even from segments of the BJP’s traditional base.
That legitimacy will not shield the movement from state resistance, though. India’s administrative apparatus has many tools for containing digital mobilization. The first is direct restriction of access through internet shutdowns. Between 2012 and 2020, BJP-governed states accounted for 501 of 637 affected districts nationwide, with shutdown probability rising sharply wherever Hindu-Muslim tensions or sustained protest activity increased. 
State governments, not the center, issue most of these shutdowns, giving the ruling party a decentralized mechanism for cutting off the platforms that memes depend on. The central administration benefits from the suppression while formal blame lands on individual state officials. 
The second tool is narrative control. India’s media landscape under Modi leans toward government-aligned framing, where dissent risks being labeled anti-national. The administration can also deploy its own digital traces and its influence over mainstream outlets to reframe the CJP as an opposition proxy or as trivial slacktivism, competing for the same attention economy that gave the movement its initial scale.
What happens next with the ongoing movement is thus an open question. The CJP has cleared the bar that stalls most leaderless movements by building a formal political infrastructure. Whether that infrastructure survives sustained administrative pressure, and whether the government’s shutdown and narrative tools prove capable of dissolving a movement built on peer reproduction, remains to be seen. Even if it survives, it’s unclear whether the CJP can convert grassroots legitimacy into electoral or policy outcomes.
Cockroaches survived millions of years not by being clever but by refusing to stop adapting. As the cockroach meme now spreading across India’s digital ecosystem suggests, this rapid adaptation is what this generation of Indian youth is showing now.

articles.title: Xi’s Shanghai Tour Offers No Relief for the Housing Crisis
articles.full_text:
Aside from making sympathetic noises about living standards, Xi offered no new wisdom or solutions.
Xi Jinping, president of China and general secretary of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP), traveled to Shanghai in mid-July. While the major reason for his trip was to open an international AI conference, he also had another priority: symbolically addressing concerns related to the distressed property market.
Xi began his Shanghai visit with an inspection tour in Huangpu District, the traditional heart of the old city of Shanghai. Huangpu is home to the Bund and its 19th century British-built buildings. Xi met local citizens and CCP officials alike, and made a point of focusing on their standard of living, rather than suggesting that they should move into newly constructed housing, often in the outer suburbs of the city or beyond.
Of all of China’s domestic priorities, home ownership and property investment has been both a boon and a bane.
Professor of Economics Kenneth Rogoff of Harvard University, in the Brookings Podcast on Economic Activity, stated in April that “real estate has been the cornerstone of the Chinese growth model, and if you include infrastructure which is closely related, it accounts for roughly a third of demand in China over a very long period. It has been the engine along with exports of China’s growth.”
Rogoff stressed that “the collapse in housing prices is a huge collapse in wealth, because Chinese citizens hold over 70 percent of their wealth in housing… the first order problem is that people feel a lot poorer and cut back their consumption accordingly.”
Deutsche Welle (DW), Germany’s state-funded international broadcaster, reported in December 2025 that the real estate market is so sensitive that in November 2025, Chinese officials “told private data providers to stop publishing home sales figures, cutting off one of the few independent windows into the current woes in the real estate market.”

articles.title: Xi Jinping’s AI Vision
articles.full_text:
Xi’s speech addressed the attendees at the World Artificial Intelligence Conference, but his real audience was the international community, and of course the United States.
China’s President Xi Jinping delivers opening remarks at the 2026 World AI Conference in Shanghai, China, July 17, 2026.
Xi Jinping, president of China and general secretary of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP), traveled to Shanghai in mid-July. Of his several missions in Shanghai, none was more important than his opening speech to the World Artificial Intelligence Conference. 
Breaking from the norm established since the first World Artificial Intelligence Conference was held in Shanghai in 2018, Xi himself, rather than a leader from the inner circles of the CCP, took the helm on July 17 and opened the conference with his thoughts. And his speech left no doubt that he has decided to take a leading role in the development of AI.
Xi’s speech addressed the attendees at the conference, but his real audience was the international community, and of course the United States, China’s chief competitor in AI development. Surprisingly, Xi began his speech by giving credit to the foreign sources that initiated the study and development of AI. 
“Seventy years ago,” Xi told the assembly, “a group of young scholars proposed the concept of artificial intelligence (AI) for the first time at the Dartmouth Workshop in New Hampshire of the United States.”
 The reference to the foreign, indeed American, creators who were the progenitors of AI is an uncharacteristic acknowledgement for a Chinese leader to make.
Xi’s nod to Western technology did not end with AI. 
“In the course of history,” Xi said, “the invention of the steam engine heralded the industrial civilization, the widespread access to electricity brightened up modern society, and the birth of the internet brought the entire world together.” 
All of these inventions originated in Europe or the United States.
While lauding the potential of AI, Xi did not shy away from the reality that much is still unknown about AI’s capabilities:
We human beings must answer the questions posed by our times: How to get along with thinking machines? How to ensure security when algorithm is part of decision-making? How to tackle ethical challenges by technologies through adaptive governance? How to realize AI for all when the divide keeps widening? These questions demand serious consideration and real answers from the whole international community.
One must not forget, however, the world in which Xi Jinping believes. The fundamental question for Xi is: How does a one-party state, which controls and where necessary censors all forms of state-owned and private media alike, all of a sudden take the reins to control a technology that has proven itself to be unpredictable? 
Xi alluded to this question. “China lays great emphasis on safety and security in AI development,” he said. “With a deep understanding of the trends and logic of AI development, we are continuously improving laws, regulations, policies, mechanisms, application norms, as well as ethical principles to make sure that AI is safe, secure and controllable, and that this fine steed of AI gallops with both speed and stability.”
It can be surmised that “stability” is the key concept here, as nothing is more precious to the CCP than a stable and content society that continues to carve out space for the party to not only survive, but thrive.
It can be argued that the entire field of AI – handing over control of key systems to a black-box algorithm – is anathema to China’s political model. Perhaps this is the very reason that China is attempting to insert itself as a global leader in AI protocols and standards. The CCP’s top brass certainly realizes that the genie is out of the bottle. AI is here and it is growing in both usage and impact. What happens when AI outflanks and outgrows China’s censors? 
Once AI has broken the levees built to keep CCP and government data and information secret, it is difficult to believe that there would not be a backlash from society at large. Therefore, the CCP needs to be able to rein it in, and control AI for its own political safety. Xi openly stated in his speech that AI must be “secure and controllable… We should put in place laws and regulations, technological monitoring, early warning and emergency response systems in order to strengthen the line of security, prevent abuses and malicious use, and ensure that AI is always under human control.”
Xi is also pushing to have the world agree on rules and regulations for AI – and, implicitly, China would leader those efforts. 
“We should enhance alignment and coordination on AI development strategies, governance rules and technical standards so as to form a consensus-based global governance framework at an early date to make this frontier technology better benefit humanity,” Xi said. “We must carry out extensive international cooperation and help Global South countries with capacity building to bridge the AI and digital divides, promote sustainable development, and prevent creating new historical injustice in AI.” 
Xi wants China to lead all of these efforts. Policymakers in free and open societies would be well advised to take note and to ensure that their transition to an AI world is on their terms, rather than on the terms of nations with differing values.
