articles.title: Johor State Election 2026: Decoding Peninsular Malaysian Politics
articles.full_text:
The Johor state election does not automatically presage a nationwide BN sweep because the results are heavily steeped in Johor’s unique local context.
In the Johor state election held on July 11, 2026, Barisan Nasional (BN) won 48 of the 56 seats, while Pakatan Harapan (PH), a coalition led by Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim, secured just eight. The results prompted observers to use the term “Blue Wave.” Is this a precursor to a major shift among voters, and could it redirect Malaysia’s political future at the federal level? Given Johor’s importance as one of the key states in Peninsular Malaysia, it is understandable that such a discussion would emerge.
Surface-level observations, however, miss the nuanced implications. The real story is not in these numbers, but in interpreting the shifts since the last election, considering the historical setting, and studying the different aspects of Johor’s constituencies – ethnic composition, degree of urbanization, and economic conditions. Only by doing so can the current state of Peninsular Malaysian politics be gauged.
Despite the “wave” headlines, there seems to be no massive “Blue Wave” driven by large-scale voter migration from PH to BN. While the 48-8 margin is indisputable, it is still worth remembering that BN already held 40 seats and the state government before the dissolution of the state assembly. 
From this perspective, the election saw them increase their existing majority by just eight seats.
Historically, Johor is the birthplace of the United Malays National Organization (UMNO) and has long served as BN’s most important support base. While BN’s nationwide popularity plummeted in 2018  – a tsunami that rattled Johor as well  – that seems to have been rock bottom. It has since simply returned to its historically formidable baseline.
Viewed from another angle, it is hard to argue that PH suffered a catastrophic loss of support. A look at vote shares and total ballots cast reveals no evidence of a massive exodus of PH voters. In fact, despite losing in seat counts, PH saw a numerical increase in its total vote count, rising from 367,525 votes in 2022 to 611,983 votes in 2026. Its share of the total vote also increased from 26.42 percent in 2022 to 32.64 percent in 2026.
The decisive factor was instead the magnitude of BN’s gains. BN’s popular vote surged from 599,753 votes, which was 43.11 percent in 2022, to 1,118,559 votes, nearly 60 percent, in 2026. This was achieved by eroding the support base of Perikatan Nasional (PN), which suffered a wipeout, losing all three of its seats and seeing its vote share plummet from over 25 percent to just around 5 percent. Put simply, voters did not defect en masse from PH to BN; rather, the political landscape reverted from its recent three-coalition fractured state back to a bipolar contest between PH and BN, favoring the ruling coalition’s machinery at the state level.
Even without a substantial swing in voter loyalty, the constituencies that did flip send a critical message. The true implications of this election can be drawn from ethnically mixed constituencies – constituencies where neither Malays nor non-Malays hold an overwhelming majority.
Comparing the seven seats PH defended against the five seats that flipped to BN reveals sharp demographic differences. The flipped seats include Jementah (N02) and Tangkak (N10) near the neighboring Melaka border; Bukit Batu (N51) on the outskirts of Johor Bahru; and Johor Jaya (N42) and Perling (N46) in the core of the state capital, Johor Bahru.
PH held its ground in seats where Malay voters constituted less than 45 percent of the electorate, but lost to BN in mixed seats where the Malay population fell within the 45-55 percent range. In Jementah (N02), for example, BN’s See Ann Giap won with 12,522 votes (46.3 percent), narrowly edging out PH’s Ng Kor Sim, who garnered 11,609 votes (42.9 percent) – a margin of just 913 votes. Similarly, in Bukit Batu (N51), BN’s Kumaran Ramakrishnan scraped a victory with 16,899 votes (47.7 percent) against PH’s Arthur Chiong Sen Sern’s 16,725 votes (47.2 percent), a thin margin of 174 votes. Furthermore, even in urban, higher-income (T20) dense areas, BN came out victorious wherever the ethnic makeup was mixed.
There was a substantial contrast in voter turnout between rural and urban districts. While the 2022 election recorded an overall turnout of 54.92 percent, participation jumped to 69.57 percent this time. A closer look at the breakdown, however, is more indicative: rural, Malay-majority (over 60 percent) areas, particularly BN incumbent strongholds, recorded higher turnouts averaging 65.7 to 68 percent. In contrast, urban PH – more precisely, Democratic Action Party (DAP) – strongholds with higher non-Malay populations lagged, averaging 60 percent.
Semi-urban seats can reflect either rural or urban characteristics depending on voter behavior. For instance, Jementah (N02) recorded 65.73 percent turnout and Tangkak (N10) recorded 67.21 percent turnout. Based on these figures, it is highly plausible that high turnout among rural-leaning Malays offset lower participation among urban-leaning non-Malays, including outstation voters who abstained, allowing rural political conditions to dominate and favor BN in the total calculation.
Interestingly, Johor Jaya (N42) – an urban seat in Johor Bahru that flipped from PH to BN – saw relatively high turnout. A local Chinese voter in this district whom the author spoke to said, “This time, support within family members is split between PH and BN.” As non-Malay voter intensity waned into ambivalence and often led to split tickets, a highly mobilized Malay voting bloc successfully pushed BN over the finish line, even without a major migration of non-Malay votes.
Meanwhile, in the rural constituencies, the consolidation of votes behind BN – and UMNO in particular – was so decisive that many races felt effectively over even before voting day. In the previous election, rural areas often saw a de facto two-way race between BN and PN. This time, internal friction between Parti Islam Se-Malaysia (PAS) and Parti Pribumi Bersatu Malaysia (Bersatu) fractured PN, rendering them unable to field candidates in all 56 seats.
Furthermore, PAS’s decision to quietly back BN significantly changed the dynamics of the race.
The most symbolic outcome of this was the collapse of Bersatu. In Bukit Kepong (N07) – a part of Pagoh, the stronghold of former Prime Minister Muhyiddin Yassin – Bersatu fielded former Chief Minister Sahruddin Jamal. Despite the roadside of Pagoh plastered with banners bearing Muhyiddin’s face to maximize his influence, BN’s Ahmad Syarie Yusof won in a landslide with 16,386 votes (61.4 percent), completely defeating Sahruddin, who only managed to gain 5,625 votes (21.1 percent). This result can be seen as an eradication of Bersatu’s foothold in its own backyard.
The defeat in Bukit Kepong (N07) illustrates the renewed primacy of the party brand in Peninsular Malaysian politics. Southeast Asian electoral politics often tilts toward the appeal of individual political personalities rather than institutional political parties. This trend had also intensified to some extent in Malaysia during the post-2018 polarization.
This time, however, the signaling power of the BN versus PH brand seems to have taken center stage. 
A Malay voter in Bukit Kepong (N07) told the author, “I don’t have any negative feelings toward Muhyiddin or the PN incumbent. But the BN brand is more important to me. The reason we supported Muhyiddin before was that he still somewhat personified the spirit of BN and UMNO.” 
This demonstrates a shift at the grassroots level: voters are acknowledging personal legacies but prioritizing party signaling or identification. When a brand’s value plummets, even former prime ministers and local heavyweights struggle to survive the battle.
This argument also extends to the effectiveness of a “poster boy” in electoral campaigns. BN strategically hid its often controversial national chairman, Deputy Prime Minister Ahmad Zahid Hamidi, choosing instead to front Chief Minister Onn Hafiz Ghazi. Effectively strategizing a slogan like “Onn Tak Onn” (a kind of word play on the colloquial Malay phrase “On tak on?” – meaning “Are we doing this or not?” – using the chief minister’s name to ask voters, “Are you with Onn?”), campaign banners featured local candidates alongside the chief minister, successfully framing the election as a referendum on the BN-led state government rather than federal politics. Conversely, PH was unable to use Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim as its focal point, resulting in his notably rare appearance on campaign materials like roadside campaign banners.
Crucially, however, what has been observed is that a poster boy only functions as a viable add-on when attached to a solid party brand. The failure of the new party Bersama – established and led by Parti Keadilan Rakyat (PKR) defector Rafizi Ramli – to gain any traction perfectly illustrates this point. Maszlee Malik’s victory for PH in Puteri Wangsa (N41) can be seen as a product of his high personal profile combined with the enduring PH brand. Onn Hafiz himself, as a descendant of UMNO founder Onn Jaafar, served as the ultimate embodiment of the party brand, which by nature boosted specific Malay voting blocs, as discussed earlier.
As a side note, the direct electoral impact of Onn’s flagship Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone (JS-SEZ) policy seems to remain difficult to quantify, with no clear correlation observed, as the affected areas saw a mix of seats where PH held strong and seats where BN flipped.
Following the political tsunami of 2018, Malaysia entered an era of fragmentation, marked by a proliferation of new political vehicles and fragmented political parties. However, the future for these micro-parties looks somewhat bleak.
Not only did the Malaysian United Democratic Alliance (MUDA) and Bersatu lose their seats, but the newly birthed Bersama also proved invisible to the electorate, despite flying its iconic yellow Kancil (the mouse-deer, an animal native to Malaysia that is often featured in local folklore) flags across the Johor Bahru area, where they fielded candidates. The party suffered crushing defeats, losing its deposits in the vast majority of the 15 seats it contested and failing to play even a substantial spoiler role for either PH or BN. As Maurice Duverger theorized, single-member district systems tend to favor a two-party system. Sustained multiparty fragmentation might be theoretically unnatural in these settings, and politics in Peninsular Malaysia, in a sense, is reverting to its normal state as far as can be observed in this state election.
The Johor state election does not automatically presage a nationwide BN sweep because the results are heavily steeped in Johor’s unique local context. Nevertheless, looking ahead to state elections in Negeri Sembilan and Melaka, and eventually the general election, Johor has provided invaluable insight into where Peninsular politics currently stands and where it is heading.
The electoral results indicate no drastic voter realignments. Rather, powered by PN’s internal dysfunction and PAS’s tactical coordination with BN, structural consolidation is reverting toward the two dominant federal coalitions: PH and BN. Third forces, often relying solely on the name recognition of their founders or leaders, are struggling for relevance, let alone the ability to dictate broader political trends. A poster boy is important, but only if there is a strong brand to build upon.
The critical variable moving forward will be voter turnout in semi-urban, ethnically mixed constituencies. If Chinese participation in urban constituencies drops as rural Malay turnout rises, these swing battlegrounds will functionally adopt rural characteristics. For PH, the battle for these semi-urban seats, especially turnout, will likely determine their fate in the end.
Before 2018, Malaysia was largely defined by a bipolar struggle between BN and the opposition. The fragmentation of the past few years may well come to be seen as an anomaly. Whether this current momentum observed in Johor toward consolidation signals that Peninsular Malaysian politics is finally entering a new stable state is a question that must be cautiously scrutinized as the next electoral battles unfold in other peninsular states and, ultimately, at the federal level in the upcoming general election.
articles.summary: The Johor state election does not automatically presage a nationwide BN sweep because the results are heavily steeped in Johor's unique local context.

articles.title: Lee Pushes AI Investment in Silicon Valley and Turns to South American Minerals
articles.full_text:
The South Korean president secured semiconductor pledges in San Francisco before turning to trade and mineral agreements in Brazil and Chile.
South Korean President Lee Jae-myung passes an honor guard during a welcome ceremony in Brasilia, Brazil, July 27, 2026.
South Korean President Lee Jae-myung is nearing the end of the longest overseas trip of his 14-month presidency, an 11-day swing that carried him from Silicon Valley’s technology corridor to the mineral-rich economies of South America. Lee, who took office in June 2025, opened the tour with investment pledges from four of the world’s leading artificial intelligence companies, then flew on to Brazil and Chile where he secured trade and critical-mineral commitments from both countries. 
In the following days, he will head to Buenos Aires, the capital of Argentina, to have a summit meeting with Argentine President Javier Milei prior to his final stop in Frankfurt, Germany next week.
The Latin American leg marked Lee’s first tour of the region. The presidential Blue House has framed the trip as part of broader “Global South diplomacy” push that is central to diversifying South Korea’s trade and diplomatic ties beyond the United States, China, and Japan. Brazil, Chile, and Argentina together form a market of some 280 million people with a combined gross domestic product of $3.7 trillion, roughly the size of the world’s seventh-largest economy, according to Seoul. Brazil and Argentina anchor Mercosur, the four-nation South American trade bloc that also includes Paraguay and Uruguay. The Lee administration has spent years trying to negotiate a trade agreement with the bloc.
Lee began the trip on July 24 with separate meetings in San Francisco with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, and Broadcom President and CEO Hock Tan. Kim Yong-beom, the policy chief for Lee, said the meetings were meant to advance South Korea’s three flagship megaprojects – a government investment push spanning semiconductors, AI data centers and physical AI that Lee announced earlier in his term. 
Speaking at the San Francisco AI Summit on July 25, Lee outlined plans for South Korea to serve as a stable supply base for AI infrastructure even amid a global chip shortage. He unveiled what his office called the San Francisco Declaration on AI, pledging that the country “will become a trusted production base and supply-chain partner for AI chips.”
South Korean and U.S. companies translated the summit into deals worth a combined $950 billion over five years, headlined by a five-year, $200 billion arrangement between Samsung Electronics and Broadcom for the supply of advanced memory chips used in AI accelerators. Lee also met with representatives of six Silicon Valley venture capital firms at an investment meetup on July 25, where the National Pension Service separately signed a memorandum of understanding with a group of global venture capital firms to build channels into Silicon Valley startups.
Lee arrived in Brazil on July 26 for a state visit at the invitation of Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. It was Lee’s fifth meeting with Lula and the first state visit by a Korean leader to Brazil since Park Geun-hye’s in 2015. The two leaders held a summit on July 27 at the Alvorada Palace where they adopted a joint statement declaring 2026 the founding year of an upgraded strategic partnership between the two countries. South Korea and Brazil signed seven memoranda of understanding spanning industrial technology, space, energy, sports, education, film, and cybersecurity. 
The leaders also agreed to form a joint working group aiming to resume long-stalled negotiations on the Korea-Mercosur trade agreement, with a target of restarting talks by December. Brazil, which holds the world’s second-largest reserves of rare earth elements at roughly 21 million tons, emerged as a central focus of Lee’s larger tour, with officials citing critical mineral supply chains among the summit’s main outcomes. 
On July 29, Lee arrived in Santiago, Chile, becoming the first South Korean president to visit Chile since Park’s South America tour 11 years ago. At a joint news conference the following day, Lee and Chilean President Jose Antonio Kast agreed to revive the South Korea-Chile Free Trade Commission for the first time in a decade and to modernize their free trade agreement, which took effect in 2004. Lee said the two sides had agreed to expand trade and investment ties in pursuit of shared growth. The two governments also signed five memoranda of understanding on critical minerals and fighting transnational crime, including a partnership that elevates a joint minerals committee to the ministerial level to help secure copper and lithium supplies worth roughly $2.1 billion a year.
Lee is scheduled to meet Argentina’s Milei on July 31 at the Casa Rosada presidential palace, following a wreath-laying ceremony at Plaza San Martín. It’s the first bilateral visit by a Korean president to Argentina in 22 years. Seoul said ahead of the meeting that the visit was expected to build a supply chain partnership around lithium, of which Argentina holds the world’s fourth-largest reserves, along with energy and food security cooperation. 
Lee is scheduled to close out the trip with a meeting with the Korean community in Frankfurt on August 2, before returning to Seoul the following day.

articles.title: South Asia’s Smaller States Push to Revive SAARC — Again
articles.full_text:
Will the region’s perpetually squabbling siblings — India and Pakistan — put aside their insecurities to make regional cooperation happen?
History seems to be repeating itself in South Asia as the region’s smaller nations once again demand the revitalization of the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC).
Delivering a speech during the Maldives’ Independence Day celebrations on July 26, Maldivian President Mohamed Muizzu urged SAARC members to return to the negotiating table, resume summits and set aside their differences for the sake of regional peace and cooperation. He added the Maldives was ready to help initiate discussions and mediate among member states.
This is not the first time Muizzu has called for SAARC’s revival. He made a similar call at the 40th Charter Day in December 2025.
Coincidentally, Bangladesh’s Foreign Minister Khalilur Rahman attended the Maldivian Independence Day ceremony as a special guest. In February, Rahman told SAARC Secretary-General Golam Sarwar that Bangladesh is committed to the organization and was ready to support its revitalization. Rahman said trade, connectivity, poverty reduction, energy, climate change, food security, education and health are areas that require regional cooperation. In April, Rahman said SAARC’s revival is an important foreign-policy objective of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s government. It was former Bangladeshi President Ziaur Rahman, the current prime minister’s father, who first formally proposed the establishment of SAARC.
The demand for SAARC’s revival is not limited to Bangladesh and the Maldives. In recent days, powerful voices in both Sri Lanka and Nepal have urged for the revitalization of the grouping.
Unsurprisingly, it is the smaller South Asian nations that are keener on SAARC. Unsurprisingly,  India seems reluctant to get the band back together. Its response to the call has been lukewarm, veering towards negative; while Pakistan supports revival, it has not publicly responded to Muizzu’s specific mediation offer.
But students of the region’s history know that the initial skepticism of the two main regional powers, in itself, is not a reason to write off the initiative.
The idea of a pan-South Asian organization is not new. In 1947, leaders of Asian nations met in New Delhi for the Asian Relations Conference to explore regional cooperation, but prospects for South Asian regional cooperation were slim due to the tensions between India and Pakistan.
However, the regional landscape changed in the late 1970s, with leadership changes in India and Pakistan, ASEAN’s formation, and global economic and security trends. These created an environment more conducive to cooperation.
In May 1980, Bangladeshi President Ziaur Rahman formally proposed the establishment of an organization that promotes South Asian economic, social, and technical cooperation. Nepal and Sri Lanka were quick to back this call, but India and Pakistan were suspicious. Both worried that this was a ploy by the other to trap them.
The historical parallels to developments today do not end there. General Ziaur Rahman came to power in 1977, following a series of events that began in a military coup in 1975 that overthrew the government of Sheikh Mujibur Rahman that India supported. The present Bangladeshi government replaced a pro-Indian regime led by Sheikh Mujibur’s daughter, Sheikh Hasina, which was toppled in 2024.
In both periods, a Bangladeshi administration that sought to redefine its relationship with India placed South Asian regional cooperation near the center of its foreign policy.
Beyond, President Rahman’s desire to normalize relations with India, several other factors like the need to mobilize regional resources to deal with an acute balance of payment crisis faced by several South Asian countries; the failure of the North-South dialogues and increasing protectionism by developed countries; and the failure of some South Asian nations like Sri Lanka to join ASEAN as members, contributed to the enthusiasm of smaller South Asian nations for regional cooperation. The Soviet military operations in Afghanistan in December 1979 and the consequent deterioration of regional security environment in South Asia made regional cooperation even more urgent.
Despite the enthusiasm of smaller nations, both India and Pakistan were initially suspicious of the Bangladeshi proposal. India feared that a regional organization will allow its smaller neighbors to raise contentious bilateral issues, even “gang up” against it, while Pakistan worried closer regional integration would further strengthen the Indian position in South Asia. Nevertheless, both countries worried about the consequences of being left out, and ultimately joined the organization.
What followed over the next four decades is well known. SAARC’s scope of action was limited from its inception because of structural and political constraints. The hostility between India and Pakistan, sometimes described as “hostility consensus,” repeatedly undermined the organization’s cohesion and effectiveness. For example, the SAARC Charter, signed in Dhaka in December 1985, was diluted to emphasize functional cooperation (economic, social, cultural, technical, scientific), while excluding contentious bilateral issues. This prevented SAARC from addressing the India-Pakistan disputes that were capable of paralyzing it. All these weakened SAARC, setting the stage for later dysfunction.
SAARC’s operational capacity too was affected by tensions between India and Pakistan. Scheduled annual heads-of-state summits have been repeatedly delayed, with no summits convened since 2014. The 2016 summit that was to be held in Islamabad was cancelled when India and its allies withdrew, alleging Pakistani involvement in an attack on an Indian army base in Kashmir.
Regional economic integration initiatives such as SAPTA (1993) and SAFTA (2004) failed to achieve stated objectives, hindered by structural economic disparities.  The dominance of India’s economy, which accounts for around 80 percent of regional GDP, has provoked concern among smaller economies, which have imposed trade barriers to protect domestic producers. Intra-regional trade stands at around 5 percent, lower than in Sub-Saharan Africa. The recent economic crises in Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Maldives, Bangladesh, and Nepal have further widened these disparities and dampened any impetus for intraregional trade.
India has increasingly pursued regional cooperation through Pakistan-free arrangements like BIMSTEC and subregional initiatives. It has also used the Indian Ocean Rim Association (IORA) for wider Indian Ocean diplomacy.
Bangladesh says it does not regard SAARC and BIMSTEC as competing choices. South Asia needs both organizations.
Despite their troubles with SAARC, no country has formally left the regional grouping.
One reason is that SAARC has achieved success in areas where Indo-Pakistani rivalries can be sidestepped. For instance, SAARC nations contributed around $22 million for a COVID-19 Emergency Fund.
And it seems that in 2026, the situation South Asian countries face is quite similar to the late 1970s. The U.S.-Israeli aggression against Iran and the spillover of the conflict to the Indian Ocean have made some South Asian countries the frontline of the conflict.
Several countries have new leaders and shattered economies. Most importantly, the recent wave of U.S. tariffs and the potential unravelling of regulations that governed global trade have made regional blocs an attractive option for smaller nations desiring bargaining power — especially after ASEAN has shown that regional groupings are excellent in dealing with both China and the U.S.
As in the late 1970s, there is incentive for almost everyone, including India, to bet on a regional bloc.
Despite cozying up to the United States for the past decade, India has been subjected to repeated tariffs by the U.S. It is possible that it will again be tariffed 100 percent for buying Russian oil – a blow that comes a few months after Washington announced it has allowed India to buy Russian oil because it was a “good actor.”
That accumulating frustration, combined with the smaller states’ renewed urgency, creates a dynamic that feels similar to the late 1970s.
The smaller South Asian nations are setting the table, laying out the plates for a family dinner, while the two eldest brothers refuse to leave their rooms. Whether India and Pakistan will eventually take their seats, as they did reluctantly in the 1980s, is uncertain. But as the crises gathering outside the door continue to mount, even the most stubborn of siblings may find that the cost of staying away has overtaken the cost of showing up.

He added the Maldives was ready to help initiate discussions and mediate among member states.

articles.title: Mongolia Signs Fuel Deal With South Korea
articles.full_text:
South Korea is now becoming a key guarantor of stability for Mongolian gas stations and aviation.
Mongolia just made a historic breakthrough by signing a deal to buy oil products from South Korea. 
Successful negotiations between Mongolian Minister of Industry and Mineral Resources Damdinnyam Gongor and South Korea’s Ministry of Trade, Industry, and Energy have resulted in an unprecedented agreement that will completely change the rules of the game in the domestic fuel market. 
For Ulaanbaatar, it’s a powerful strategic move toward energy independence. Currently, Russia supplies over 90 percent of Mongolia’s refined petroleum products, with the rest purchased from China.
According to the agreement reached on July 30, Seoul will supply Mongolia with 50,000 tons of high-quality petroleum products monthly: 10,000 tons of jet fuel, 20,000 tons of AI-92 gasoline (covering over 33 percent of the country’s total monthly demand), and 20,000 tons of diesel fuel (about 20 percent of the monthly requirement for Mongolia’s logistics and agricultural sector). 
The fuel agreement follows South Korean President Lee Jae-myung’s state visit to Mongolia from July 9-11, which saw the two sides proclaim “a ‘New Golden Era’ of Mongolia-Korea relations.” Lee’s visit resulted in a bevy of agreements, including near-finalization of a Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) that will see tariff reductions. Trade and investment were major themes, in keeping with Mongolia’s broader push to diversify its economy away from a reliance on Russia and China.
Now the fuel purchase joins the 21 cooperation agreements signed during Lee’s visit.
Mongolia’s fuel supply has been under new pressure, both because of global supply chain difficulties stemming from disruptions to the Strait of Hormuz and because of Russia’s tightening fuel supply. Mongolia is nearly totally reliant on Russian fuel imports, but Russia itself is facing shortages amid Ukrainian drone strikes on petroleum refining facilities. The crisis has forced Russia to request fuel from neighboring Kazakhstan, according to Reuters, along with banning exports of diesel. Other countries reliant on Russia for fuel imports, including Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan, have had to implement emergency fuel management measures.
At the same time, the summer season, peak tourism, and large-scale agricultural work have increased fuel demand within Mongolia by two to three times. To avoid shortages and severe dependence on traditional suppliers, the Mongolian government is rapidly diversifying its imports. In parallel with the South Korean contract, Mongolia has already secured an emergency supply of another 6,000 tons of gasoline from China. 
Authorities are resolute that there will be no shortage, and the domestic market will receive a reliable safety net of high-quality fuel. And with the new agreement, South Korea is becoming a key guarantor of stability for Mongolian gas stations and aviation.

articles.title: For the Arakan Army, Recognition Must Be Earned
articles.full_text:
The Arakan Army’s quest for international recognition should be tied to Rohingya rights and accountability.
Recently, Human Rights Watch published a distressing investigative report, tellingly titled “Skeletons and Skulls Scattered Everywhere.” The report confirmed that the Arakan Army had massacred at least 170 Rohingya civilians, including 90 children, and likely killed or wounded hundreds more in the village of Hoyyar Siri (Htan Shauk Khan in Burmese) in the Buthidaung Township of Myanmar’s Rakhine State on May 2, 2024. 
This constitutes only a small fraction of the Arakan Army’s record of human rights violations against the Rohingyas. Since the ethnic armed organization (EAO) has wrested control of much of the Rakhine State in 2023-2024, it has expelled more than 150,000 Rohingyas into Bangladesh, committed war crimes — massacres, rape, and arson — against Rohingya civilians; subjected them to severe restrictions, extortion, and forced conscription; and even banned the use of the word “Rohingya” upon the threat of harsh penalty. In fact, Major General Twan Mrat Naing, the commander-in-chief of the Arakan Army and the Chairman of the United League of Arakan (ULA), had publicly denied the distinct identity of the Rohingyas, terming them as “Bengalis.”
Thus, while the Arakan Army is deliberately refusing to recognize the distinct identity of the Rohingyas, who constituted between 25 and 30 percent of the population of Rakhine State before the 2017 “cleansing operations,” it is seeking international recognition for its de facto control over Rakhine State. 
Using the geostrategic importance of Rakhine State as a leverage, the Arakan Army is trying to legitimize its territorial and administrative control over state by seeking recognition from external actors with political, economic, security, and strategic interests in the region, particularly China, India, Bangladesh, and the United States. Rakhine State holds substantial reserves of oil and natural gas, has strategic access to the Indian Ocean, hosts important Chinese and Indian geo-strategic projects, and often serves as a conduit or transit route for regional non-state armed actors. Using these factors as bargaining chips, the Arakan Army is trying to attain international recognition.
In international law, the issue of the recognition of a new state or a new government is highly complex. Since the Arakan Army has not yet made a formal declaration of independence, the question of the recognition of an independent Rakhine State is moot from the viewpoint of international law. Hence, the question is about the recognition of its government. So far, while the Arakan Army has not yet declared independence, it has formed its own government for Rakhine State, termed the Arakan People’s Revolutionary Government (APRG), which is essentially controlled by the ULA. Meanwhile, the Rakhine State Government, located in the capital Sittwe, is formally under the Tatmadaw-backed Myanmar Union Government. Thus, Rakhine State currently has two rival governments.
The situation on the ground is as follows: the Arakan Army controls approximately 90 percent of the territory of Rakhine State, along with the Paletwa Township of Chin State. In these territories, the APRG acts as the de facto government. The military-backed Rakhine State Government remains the de jure government of the state, but its de facto authority is currently restricted to the state capital Sittwe, the strategic port of Kyaukphyu, and parts of the Ann Township which the military controls. 
As long as the Rakhine State Government retains control of Sittwe, it is unlikely that any foreign state would grant de jure recognition to the APRG. However, a number of states, including China, India, and Bangladesh, have engaged with the Arakan Army in order to safeguard their interests in Rakhine State, and international institutions, particularly humanitarian actors, need to engage with the Arakan Army to avert a humanitarian crisis in the region. This creates the possibility that the Arakan Army may attempt to secure de facto recognition of its government from these states and institutions.
Whether Beijing, New Delhi, Dhaka, or any other capital would extend de facto recognition to the APRG is contingent upon the dynamics of their relations with the Tatmadaw-controlled Myanmar Union Government, the trajectory of the Myanmar civil war, and the perceptions of the urgency of their interests in Rakhine State. However, before granting any sort of recognition to the APRG, states and international institutions must take into account the following factors.
First, Rakhine State is still engulfed by war, and the APRG’s control over the region is not undisputed. The Myanmar Union Government is still engaged in an intense war against the Arakan Army, and Chin EAOs are opposed to continued Arakan Army control of Paletwa Township. Granting recognition to such an entity, even if only de facto, would be premature.
Second, the Arakan Army has displayed latent expansionist and confrontational tendencies in its actions toward other actors in the region. Its occupation of Paletwa Township has created fictions with Chin EAOs, while its actions toward Bangladesh, including repeated abductions of Bangladeshi citizens, extraction of ransom from the hostages, seizure of Bangladesh-bound vessels, imposition of illicit taxation on Bangladeshi traders, and killing of Bangladeshi citizens, have generated unease in the country. Unless the Arakan Army adopts a more moderate and conciliatory attitude, granting even de facto recognition to the ARPG would only embolden its reckless behavior and ultimately be counterproductive.
Finally, the Arakan Army has so far demonstrated no inclination to build a democratic, inclusive, and law-governed polity by ensuring the rights of all ethnic, racial, and religious communities in Myanmar. It has not only violated the rights of the long-suffering Rohingyas with impunity, it has blatantly denied the existence of a distinct Rohingya identity and effective dehumanized them by propagating the narrative that the Rohingya are “Bengali immigrants” to Rakhine State. Also, the Arakan Army has subjected other minorities, including the Chakmas and the Chin, to human rights violations. Under these circumstances, granting even de facto recognition to the APRG would be a mistake from both moral and pragmatic perspectives.
The international community and particularly the regional states should make any sort of recognition of the APRG contingent upon the Arakan Army’s recognition of the Rohingyas’ distinct identity, its commitment to safe, voluntary, dignified, and sustainable repatriation of all Rohingya refugees, its dedication to the creation of a democratic, inclusive, and law-governed polity, and its pledge to moderate its behaviour towards regional actors. This would go a long way in ensuring the stability of the region and a sustained peace in Rakhine State.

articles.title: Tajikistan Denies a Clothing Ban Its Police Keep Enforcing
articles.full_text:
A rumor with one traceable source drew an official rebuttal in Dushanbe that buried its documented enforcement.
On July 29, Tajikistan’s Committee on Religion, Regulation of Traditions, Celebrations, and Ceremonies told Asia-Plus, the country’s only remaining major independent media outlet, that the country has adopted no law banning beards or the hijab, and that foreign assessments of Tajik religious freedom rest on unreliable sources. The denial followed a week of Russian-language reports announcing that Dushanbe had outlawed hijabs, beards, and Arab-style dress.
The reports seem to run back to a single post. On July 27, the Uzbek site Nuz.uz reported that Tajik authorities were tightening restrictions on clothing treated as alien to Tajik culture, singling out black hijabs. The report cited unnamed local sources. Lenta.ru, Trud, RBC, Fontanka, and outlets in Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan republished the report within a day, promoting what appears to be an enforcement campaign into a new law. 
Nezavisimaya Gazeta traced the wording back further, to identical posts from Instagram accounts presenting themselves as legal advisers that appeared a day before Nuz.uz, and found no Tajik-language coverage of the subject dated from 2026. Asia-Plus added that several outlets had credited the claim to Asia-Plus, which had published nothing of the kind.
The committee’s denial is narrowly accurate and largely beside the point. 
The law it declines to mention passed two years ago. Article 18 of the Law on the Ordering of Traditions, Celebrations, and Ceremonies, in force since June 2024, bars importing, selling, promoting, and wearing in public any clothing that does not correspond to national culture. It does not define what that means. As Asia-Plus noted when the law was first published, it attaches no penalty to that clause either; the fines of up to 100,000 somoni ($10,800) in the accompanying administrative code amendments cover weddings, funerals, and pilgrimage rituals instead.
This is where police discretion comes in. RFE/RL reported on July 26 that a trader in Bokhtar, held for three days over his beard and fined 180 somoni ($18), now sends officers a weekly photograph of his shaved face. Two other men said police shaved them by force and released them without charge. An official at a passport office in Khatlon said applicants with beards are told to shave, that each case is logged, and that the names go into monthly reports tracking men’s facial hair and women’s religious dress. In May, the women’s affairs committee in Rudaki district posted photographs from a village-by-village campaign steering women away from foreign clothing, then deleted them.
None of that required new legislation. Tajikistan has been a U.S. Country of Particular Concern on religious freedom since 2016, and USCIRF’s May country update found the 2024 law being enforced through campaigns against dress deemed foreign to national culture, including school visits in February. Police forcibly shaved some 13,000 men as far back as 2015, when no clothing law existed at all. A prohibition that names neither the specific offense nor the punishment can be applied by any officer and denied by any ministry.
The clothing rules are one piece of a much larger fight. Dushanbe banned the Islamic Revival Party of Tajikistan (IRPT) as an extremist organization in 2015, handed life sentences to its leaders or pushed them into exile, and has since jailed journalists, lawyers, and bloggers on the same charges. The framing has paid off. Sharing the region’s longest border with Afghanistan has made Tajikistan a durable recipient of Western counterterrorism and border-security money. As Edward Lemon of the Oxus Society argued, U.S. training helped build a coercive apparatus that Dushanbe then turned on its own citizens, most visibly during the 2022 crackdown in Gorno-Badakhshan. Overstating the threat buys both funding and the latitude to use it at home.
Uzbekistan banned face coverings in 2023, and Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan followed in 2025. Russian media outlets have amplified each of these measures since Moscow’s post-Crocus Hall migration crackdown began, because the story is useful at home: proof for Russian audiences that the states supplying their labor migrants are policing their own Muslims – and so should Moscow.

Lenta.ru, Trud, RBC, Fontanka, and outlets in Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan republished the report within a day, promoting what appears to be an enforcement campaign into a new law. 
Nezavisimaya Gazeta traced the wording back further, to identical posts from Instagram accounts presenting themselves as legal advisers that appeared a day before Nuz.uz, and found no Tajik-language coverage of the subject dated from 2026. Asia-Plus added that several outlets had credited the claim to Asia-Plus, which had published nothing of the kind.
The committee’s denial is narrowly accurate and largely beside the point. 
The law it declines to mention passed two years ago. Article 18 of the Law on the Ordering of Traditions, Celebrations, and Ceremonies, in force since June 2024, bars importing, selling, promoting, and wearing in public any clothing that does not correspond to national culture. It does not define what that means. As Asia-Plus noted when the law was first published, it attaches no penalty to that clause either; the fines of up to 100,000 somoni ($10,800) in the accompanying administrative code amendments cover weddings, funerals, and pilgrimage rituals instead.
This is where police discretion comes in. RFE/RL reported on July 26 that a trader in Bokhtar, held for three days over his beard and fined 180 somoni ($18), now sends officers a weekly photograph of his shaved face. Two other men said police shaved them by force and released them without charge. An official at a passport office in Khatlon said applicants with beards are told to shave, that each case is logged, and that the names go into monthly reports tracking men’s facial hair and women’s religious dress. In May, the women’s affairs committee in Rudaki district posted photographs from a village-by-village campaign steering women away from foreign clothing, then deleted them.
None of that required new legislation. Tajikistan has been a U.S. Country of Particular Concern on religious freedom since 2016, and USCIRF’s May country update found the 2024 law being enforced through campaigns against dress deemed foreign to national culture, including school visits in February. Police forcibly shaved some 13,000 men as far back as 2015, when no clothing law existed at all. A prohibition that names neither the specific offense nor the punishment can be applied by any officer and denied by any ministry.
The clothing rules are one piece of a much larger fight. Dushanbe banned the Islamic Revival Party of Tajikistan (IRPT) as an extremist organization in 2015, handed life sentences to its leaders or pushed them into exile, and has since jailed journalists, lawyers, and bloggers on the same charges. The framing has paid off. Sharing the region’s longest border with Afghanistan has made Tajikistan a durable recipient of Western counterterrorism and border-security money. As Edward Lemon of the Oxus Society argued, U.S. training helped build a coercive apparatus that Dushanbe then turned on its own citizens, most visibly during the 2022 crackdown in Gorno-Badakhshan. Overstating the threat buys both funding and the latitude to use it at home.
Uzbekistan banned face coverings in 2023, and Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan followed in 2025. Russian media outlets have amplified each of these measures since Moscow’s post-Crocus Hall migration crackdown began, because the story is useful at home: proof for Russian audiences that the states supplying their labor migrants are policing their own Muslims – and so should Moscow.
On July 29, Tajikistan’s Committee on Religion, Regulation of Traditions, Celebrations, and Ceremonies told Asia-Plus, the country’s only remaining major independent media outlet, that the country has adopted no law banning beards or the hijab, and that foreign assessments of Tajik religious freedom rest on unreliable sources. The denial followed a week of Russian-language reports announcing that Dushanbe had outlawed hijabs, beards, and Arab-style dress.
The reports seem to run back to a single post. On July 27, the Uzbek site Nuz.uz reported that Tajik authorities were tightening restrictions on clothing treated as alien to Tajik culture, singling out black hijabs. The report cited unnamed local sources. Lenta.ru, Trud, RBC, Fontanka, and outlets in Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan republished the report within a day, promoting what appears to be an enforcement campaign into a new law.
articles.summary: A rumor with one traceable source drew an official rebuttal in Dushanbe that buried its documented enforcement.

articles.title: Transaction or Transformation? Inside the Russia-North Korea Relationship
articles.full_text:
How transactional is the massive shift in their relations and how sensitive is it to the Ukraine war?
In this episode of The Diplomat’s Asia Geopolitics Podcast, hosts Ankit Panda and Katie Putz examine the status of the Russia-North Korea partnership. Since the signing of a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership Treaty in 2024, the two have held three strategic dialogues, the most recent in late July in Moscow. How transactional is the massive shift in their relations and how sensitive is it to the Ukraine war? And what does China — which has its own nuanced relations with North Korea and Russia — think about the growing closeness between Moscow and Pyongyang?

articles.title: Japan’s Intelligence Reform Has a Counterintelligence Problem
articles.full_text:
As the Takaichi administration strives to strengthen Japan’s intelligence capabilities, it’s important to build up counterintelligence capabilities too.
In order to deal with a worsening regional security environment, Japan is stepping up its intelligence capabilities. Since establishing the National Intelligence Council (NIC) this summer, Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae acknowledged the threat caused by leaks of sensitive technology to foreign intelligence services. 
“We will continue discussions on ‘enhancing foreign intelligence collection’ and ‘strengthening the prevention of improper foreign influence’ while maintaining a balance with the people’s ‘liberty and human rights,’” she said at a recent press conference. 
As Japan continues its intelligence reforms, the government must also consider how to strengthen its counterintelligence capabilities. This will impact not only the development of a Japanese foreign intelligence service, but also Japanese aspirations to play a larger role in intelligence liaison relationships with friends and allies like the U.S. and its Five Eyes partnership. It is critical that Japanese policymakers strengthen Japan’s ability to defeat foreign espionage.
Counterintelligence is a critical part to the broader intelligence mission. According to James Olson, formerly the head of the CIA’s counterintelligence section, counterintelligence is “all the measures a nation takes to protect its citizens, secrets, and technology from foreign spies.” 
At first glance, this seems to primarily refer to the groups like Olson’s former organization at CIA or the counterintelligence section of the National Security Branch of the FBI. But counterintelligence also includes organizations like the Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States (CFIUS), which provides oversight of business acquisitions between American and foreign companies. There is also the Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency (DCSA), which investigates the suitability of a person to be granted access to classified information. Counterintelligence also includes counterespionage, which are activities used to penetrate, defeat, and manipulate foreign intelligence services. This creates an understanding of adversarial services, and create space for one’s own intelligence operations. What unites all of these activities and organizations is their ultimate objective being the defense of the state against foreign intelligence services.
Japan’s counterintelligence capabilities are minimal but like the broader intelligence community they have been getting stronger. Japan has two agencies that are broadly focused on countering foreign elements within Japan. The first is the National Police Agency (NPA), which is responsible for supervising the prefectural police forces in investigating criminal activity in Japan, including cyber crimes and terrorism. The second is the Public Security Intelligence Agency (PSIA), which also collects information on terrorist targets, which historically also included communist subversion. Together these are the main agencies responsible for protecting Japan’s domestic security.
Japan does not currently have a comprehensive anti-espionage law. The primary law that touches on counterintelligence is the Act on the Protection of Specially Designated Secrets. Passed in December 2013, the law allows Japanese government agencies to limit access to information “which is publicly undisclosed and which is particularly required to be kept secret due to the risk of causing severe damage to Japan’s national security.” The law also says that unauthorized disclosure of covered information can result in incarceration up to ten years. 
To strengthen Japan’s counterintelligence regulations, the Takaichi administration supports passing a law requiring the registration of foreign agents in Japan. Like its counterparts in the United States, the law would strengthen Japanese counterintelligence through tracking the activities of foreign intelligence officers and agents and deter espionage through prosecution.
However, there remains important regulatory and institutional work that needs to be done in order for Japanese counterintelligence to be successful. The first is clearly establishing what kind of information is and is not covered by anti-espionage laws. Japan is an open society and generally protects the free flow of information in public. But states like China have exploited this openness and conduct significant open-source intelligence (OSINT) collection, especially against technical and scientific targets. According to scholars, China engages in a broad spectrum of collection activities, from “scanning technical literature to analyzing patents, reverse engineering product samples, and capturing conversations at scientific meetings. Nothing is overlooked.” Given the threat posed by China and OSINT collection, Japan should create a legal definition of covered information that both defends Japanese national security, but also protects civil liberties.
Although intelligence oversight is important to any state, it is especially acute in Japan. In the first half of the 20th century, the Imperial Japanese government strictly controlled the dissemination of information. This fear of political repression was instrumental to defeating postwar efforts to establish a Japanese version of the CIA. These concerns are still prevalent in Japan some seven decades on. Social Democratic Party lawmaker Fukushima Mizuho said that that the new NIC “infringes upon the right to privacy and other rights and paves the way for a surveillance society.” To address concerns about abuses by intelligence agencies, Japan should consider creating legislative committees dedicated to intelligence and provide oversight. Through legislative hearings and control over funding, a Diet Committee on Intelligence would provide public oversight of counterintelligence enforcement activities.
Finally, counterintelligence needs to be inculcated across the Japanese intelligence community. Most of the Takaichi administration’s intelligence reforms have been focused on centralizing operations in the Kantei. While this may be important to prevent stovepiping and turf battles, the counterintelligence mission cannot be siloed in one independent agency. Intelligence benefits from compartmentalization, especially through authority that enforces that need-to-know principle is necessary. It would also be easier to allow each intelligence agency to conduct its own counterespionage operations, as they have the best insights on how to manipulate their intelligence targets. While centralization has been a primary outcome of the Takaichi administration’s intelligence reforms, not all aspects of the counterintelligence mission can benefit from this perspective.
The Takaichi administration should be congratulated for its efforts to strengthen its intelligence capabilities. Counterintelligence has received less attention but is extremely important to the broader strengthening of Japanese intelligence. Its primary objective is protecting Japanese intelligence, whether it be through recruiting agents, hacking into secured systems, or old-fashioned break-ins. But counterintelligence’s offensive aspect is also important to understanding foreign adversary operations in Japan and creating space for Japan’s own intelligence operations. Japan also needs to decide how to both carry out this mission while also respecting important democratic norms protecting free speech and expression. Strengthening its counterintelligence capabilities through new legislative developments and establishing institutions will be critical if Japan hopes to achieve its goal of intelligence reform.

articles.title: Redesigning International Order for a G-Minus World
articles.full_text:
This is the age of hyper-multipolarity, where every plausible steering group is missing something essential.
Leaders pose for a photo at the 52nd G7 summit in Evian, France, June 16, 2026.
Debates about international order usually begin with the same question: who will lead next? Will the United States recover its authority? Will China mature into a responsible provider of public goods? Will some concert of major powers manage the transition?
The question is familiar and increasingly misleading. The defining condition of this century is not a clean transfer of hegemony from one state to another. It is the erosion of the possibility that any single state, or compact group of great powers, can supply order for everyone else.
We live in a G-minus world. The term does not simply mean that leadership is absent, as in a G-zero world. It means that every plausible steering group is missing something essential. Military reach, manufacturing capacity, financial credibility, technological innovation, demographic weight, regulatory authority, and political legitimacy are distributed across different actors. The United States remains pre-eminent in several domains, but it depends on production networks it does not control. China is central to global manufacturing and trade, but lacks the alliance structure and financial trust to underwrite a universal order. The European Union can set standards, but cannot by itself secure the system it regulates. India, Brazil, Indonesia, Saudi Arabia, and other consequential powers cannot be treated as rule-takers, yet they do not form a coherent governing coalition.
This is more than multipolarity. It is hyper-multipolarity: power fragmented not only among states, but across domains. Strength in one arena no longer converts automatically into authority in another.
The older theory of hegemonic stability assumed that a dominant state would supply public goods because it possessed both the capacity and the incentive to do so. Today, those two dimensions have separated. The cost of underwriting open markets, dispute settlement, maritime security, financial stability, and crisis response has risen, while the domestic political return has become less certain. Great powers are therefore tempted not only to withdraw from order, but to extract from it, through tariffs, sanctions, coercive finance, and the weaponization of interdependence.
The response cannot be to ask middle powers to become a substitute hegemon. They lack the resources, and a coalition assigned hegemonic burdens would reproduce the same incentive problem on a smaller base. The more promising question is different: how can institutions make cooperation the rational choice even when no actor can command the system?
Recent experience provides three useful answers.
First, the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership survived the United States’ withdrawal from its predecessor. The remaining members preserved high-standard rules, brought the agreement into force, and later admitted the United Kingdom. The result is not a replacement for the global trading system. It is something more practical: a functioning arrangement that creates benefits for members and opportunity costs for outsiders.
Second, when the World Trade Organization (WTO) Appellate Body became unable to hear appeals, a group of WTO members initiated the Multi-Party Interim Appeal Arbitration Arrangement. More than 60 WTO members now participate, and the mechanism has produced actual arbitration outcomes. It is an imperfect bridge, but it demonstrates that institutional function need not wait for unanimity.
Third, the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) binds 15 politically diverse economies representing roughly 30 percent of global output and population. RCEP is less ambitious than the CPTPP in several areas, but that is partly the point. ASEAN’s central role and the agreement’s differentiated obligations made cooperation possible among states that would not accept a single power’s blueprint.
These cases suggest three design principles for a G-minus world.
The first is modularity. The next order will not be one grand covenant. It will be a set of independent but connectable modules: digital trade, critical minerals, carbon accounting, AI governance, dispute settlement, supply chain resilience, financial transparency, maritime safety, and public health. Each module must be useful on its own and more valuable when linked to others.
The second is differentiated participation. Institutions should abandon the fiction that every participant must assume identical obligations at the same speed. A state may be a core member in digital trade, a partial participant in supply chain cooperation, and an observer in security discussions. Graduated participation is not institutional weakness. It is how diverse states enter cooperation without surrendering all autonomy at once.
The third is visible benefit. Cooperation fails when costs are immediate and gains are abstract. Good institutional design front-loads practical value: faster customs treatment, mutual certification, shared stockpiles, access to trusted markets, lower financing costs, usable dispute resolution, and credible insurance against disruption. The institution becomes durable when governments can show that participation pays.
This also clarifies what democratic multilateralism should mean. Democracies do not have a monopoly on benefits to participation, and non-democracies offer genuine incentives to engagement: infrastructure finance, energy, market access, security assistance, and diplomatic protection. An incentive is not a bribe; it is what economists model as self-interest. The difference should lie in structure. Patron-client incentives are discretionary and asymmetric. An incentive-based democratic institution should be rules-based, reciprocal, transparent, contestable, and open to additional participants that willingly agree to abide by those rules.
The goal is not to restore liberal internationalism at its imagined peak. That order was never as universal or benign as its defenders remember. A more realistic objective is a multilateral-enough world: enough rules that disputes do not default to coercion; enough openness that smaller economies can reach scale; enough redundancy that one institution’s paralysis does not become system-wide failure; and enough predictability that governments and firms can plan.
Waiting for Washington to return to a leadership role and waiting for Beijing to become responsible are mirror versions of the same mistake: both entrust order to power. In a G-minus world, great power companionship and permission are optional. Small states and middle powers cannot replace hegemony, but they can build around its absence. The task is to stop asking who will rule the international system and instead start designing a system that states will choose to remain in.
This essay is one of four to emerge from discussions at an international conference jointly organized by the Seoul Forum for International Affairs and the Hairan Series of Korea University’s Institute for Interdisciplinary Unification Studies, “Democratic Multilateralism at the Edge,” held in Seoul on April 20, 2026.
